create_video: Create a video: a slideshow from a list of pictures (each shown for a few seconds), or a simple clip of a colour for a duration. Writes a new .mp4 next to the inputs; never overwrites. (arguments: images, seconds, color, duration, width)

photo_metadata: Read a photo's embedded EXIF metadata: the camera and lens, the date and time it was taken, exposure, aperture, ISO, focal length, and the GPS location if one is recorded. Use for 'when was this photo taken', 'does this picture contain my location', 'which camera took it'. JPEG and TIFF. Read-only; the file is not changed. (arguments: path)

generate_image: Make a new picture from a text description, or change a photo the way a description says (from_photo, e.g. 'make it snowy', 'as a watercolour'), drawn locally by stable-diffusion.cpp. Describe it in English. Saves a PNG and returns its path. (arguments: prompt, avoid, size, steps, seed, output, from_photo, strength)

convert_media: Convert an audio, video or image file to another format (mp3, ogg, opus, wav, flac, m4a, mp4, webm, gif, png, jpg, webp), optionally resizing to a width. Writes a new file next to the original; never overwrites. (arguments: path, to, width)

train.say: Install and remove apps.
train.positives_desc: install_app: Search Flathub for an app, or install / remove one for this user by its app ID (e.g. org.videolan.VLC, from a search). Installing and removing need the 'app-install-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, query, app_id)

negatives.desc: list_apps: List the applications installed on this machine, optionally filtered by a search term, so a request to open something can be answered with what actually exists rather than a guess. (arguments: search)

install_model: Download a named model into the local Ollama. Takes an explicit model name and never picks one by itself - call recommend_model first and install only what the user agreed to. Warns rather than refuses when the model looks larger than available memory. This downloads gigabytes and needs the network. (arguments: name)

android_device: An Android phone connected with USB debugging (adb). devices: which are connected; info: model, Android version, battery, storage; screenshot: save the phone's screen as a PNG; apps: installed apps (query filters); push: copy a file to the phone (to, default /sdcard/Download); pull: copy a file from the phone; open_url: open a web link on the phone. Requires 'phone-control-enabled'. (arguments: action, serial, path, to, url, query, output)

default_apps: Show or change which application opens a kind of file - by MIME type ('application/pdf'), extension ('.pdf', 'mp4') or an example file - or the default web browser (target 'browser'). Use for 'what opens PDFs', 'make VLC open my videos', 'set Firefox as my default browser'. Changing a default requires the 'default-apps-enabled' consent key; showing one does not. (arguments: target, action, app)

manage_triggers: Arm, list, or remove automatic rules that run a Chronoa action when a perception matches - for example, notify when the battery sense reports low. A rule names one already-whitelisted skill; it cannot run an arbitrary command or an LLM-authored prompt. Listing needs no permission; arming or disarming requires the 'trigger-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, name, sense, match_mode, substring, keywords, actuator, arguments, cooldown_seconds, event_type, source, params, ask_first, retry_policy, debounce_seconds)

lan_phone: Find phones on the SAME Wi-Fi network, using the KDE Connect protocol directly - so it works without KDE Connect or GSConnect installed. 'devices': what announced itself on this network in the last few seconds (phones, tablets, other computers). 'announce': make this computer findable by a phone's KDE Connect app. 'status': what this computer can and cannot do on the LAN. 'pair': what the pairing half of the protocol is and why it is not here. Needs the 'lan-phone-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, seconds)

cleanup_apply: Actually free the disk space cleanup_report measured: empty your cache folder, or remove Flatpak runtimes no app uses. Both are recoverable or provably unused. Requires the 'cleanup-enabled' consent key. The system log is not here - that needs root, which Chronoa cannot ask for from inside a tool call. (arguments: target)

train.say: Dissect traffic into protocol fields.
train.positives_desc: dissect_traffic: Capture traffic on an interface and dissect it into protocol fields with tshark, Wireshark's command-line engine: which protocols are actually on the wire, and for a filter, the specific fields - TLS handshake type and SNI, DNS query names, HTTP host. This is the companion to capture_packets: that one reads packets as they cross, this one says what they are. Filters use the same grammar as both tools. Reads packet contents, so it needs the same permission as capture_packets. Writes nothing to disk. (arguments: interface, filter, packets, seconds)

negatives.desc: ir_remote: Send and receive infrared remote-control codes, and build or read the pulse-space timings themselves. 'devices': is there IR hardware here (most machines have none, and that is a true answer). 'encode': turn an address and command into the NEC or RC-6 timings that would carry them. 'decode': turn timings into a code. 'send': transmit a code through an IR device. 'receive': capture a button press and decode it. Needs the 'ir-remote-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, protocol, address, command, timings, seconds)

phone_remote: Press keys on the paired phone as a Bluetooth keyboard: 'press' the camera 'shutter' (takes a photo in the camera app), play_pause, next, previous, volume_up/down, mute; or 'type' text into whatever field is focused on the phone. The phone must have paired 'Chronoa Remote'. Requires the 'phone-remote-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, key, text)

bridge_topology: Show which network interfaces are bridges, exactly which interfaces are enslaved to each one, and which are standalone. Answers 'is this interface actually plugged into the bridge it should be', which is the usual reason a network that reported no errors carries no traffic. Read from /sys so it needs no privileges and cannot be half-applied. Reports the plumbing, not whether traffic flows. Covers this network namespace only. (arguments: bridge)

bluetooth_gatt: Read what a paired Bluetooth Low Energy device says about itself - a watch's or headset's battery, a heart-rate strap's live reading, which services a band offers. 'list': every paired device and whether it speaks this protocol. 'services': what one exposes. 'read': one stored value. 'listen': a live reading of something the device only pushes, e.g. heart rate - 'nothing arrived' is the truthful answer when the device is not measuring. Speakers, headphones and car stereios are older Bluetooth and expose nothing here, which is a true answer, not a failure; wearables, bands, straps, smart tags and thermometers answer. Needs 'bluetooth-gatt-enabled' and the device must be connected. (arguments: action, device, seconds, characteristic)

capture_packets: Watch packets crossing one network interface for a few seconds, and report tcpdump's one-line-per-packet summaries: who sent to whom, which protocol, how long, and the TCP flags. This reads packet contents on the wire - it is the one thing in this package that does - so it is gated separately and shows no payload text. Bounded by packet count, seconds and output rows. Read-only: it captures and prints, and changes nothing. (arguments: interface, packets, seconds, filter)

json_query: Ask questions about the shape of a JSON document: what keys it has, what a field contains, how many entries an array has, or the sum/unique/sorted values of an array. Give either a file path or paste the document itself. (arguments: path, document, field, operation, of)

lan_phone: Find phones on the SAME Wi-Fi network, using the KDE Connect protocol directly - so it works without KDE Connect or GSConnect installed. 'devices': what announced itself on this network in the last few seconds (phones, tablets, other computers). 'announce': make this computer findable by a phone's KDE Connect app. 'status': what this computer can and cannot do on the LAN. 'pair': what the pairing half of the protocol is and why it is not here. Needs the 'lan-phone-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, seconds)

train.say: what timers do I have running?
train.positives_desc: set_timer: Set a countdown timer that sends a desktop notification when it finishes; list pending timers, say how much time is left, add or take off time, pause, resume, reset to the original length, and cancel. With one timer pending, 'my timer' needs no id. The countdown is owned by systemd, so it fires even if the assistant is closed. It is refused rather than silently accepted when systemd is unavailable, because a timer recorded as pending that will never fire is the same lie as a camera reported as disabled when it is not. (arguments: action, seconds, label, id)

negatives.desc: scheduled_tasks: What is scheduled to run on this machine: your crontab, the system crontab and /etc/cron.d, and both the system and your systemd timers. Each source is reported separately and one that cannot be read says so, because a machine can have no user crontab and still have nine timers. Reading what the machine has scheduled describes the machine rather than the person's world, so it needs no permission. Nothing is scheduled, changed or removed by asking. (arguments: source)

autostart_entries: Report everything on this machine that starts automatically: the autostart .desktop files in this user's home and /etc/xdg, the enabled systemd user units and timers, and the crontab. Use for 'what starts automatically', 'what runs at login', 'what is scheduled', 'why does this thing keep running', 'what did I set to start on its own'. Honours Hidden, OnlyShowIn and NotShowIn, and says 'cannot tell' rather than guessing when the desktop is unknown - which is the normal state outside a login session. Read-only; nothing is enabled, disabled or changed.

check_units: Check whether systemd unit files are valid and say what is wrong with them - a missing ExecStart binary, an unknown key, a dependency that does not exist - by running systemd-analyze verify on just the units you name. With no unit named, lists the services this machine has. This is a static check of the file: it does not know whether a dependency is down or a path is mounted, so a clean report does not promise the service will start. Reading only; nothing is started, stopped or changed. (arguments: unit)

list_services: List system services with their load and active state, optionally filtered by name, newest state first for anything running. Reports UNKNOWN on a machine that is not systemd-managed. (arguments: name_filter, failed_only)

set_sleep_inhibit: Report what is currently holding the machine awake, or take a bounded hold so it does not sleep for a while, or release ours. Use for 'keep it awake while I...' - a long install, a backup, a test run. Scoped and self-lapsing; to change the machine's idle timeout permanently use set_screensaver instead. Gated by 'sleep-inhibit-enabled' consent key; reporting needs no such permission. (arguments: action, reason, seconds)

binary_hardening: Report whether a binary is hardened: PIE, RELRO, full RELRO (BIND_NOW), stack canary and no-execute stack, each with what it stops. Use for 'is /path/to/this safe to run', 'is this binary hardened', 'does this have a stack canary', 'is this ASLR enabled'. Works on executables and shared libraries alike, and says 'not applicable' where a property genuinely has no answer rather than reporting it as missing. Read-only; nothing is loaded or written. (arguments: path)

list_containers: List this machine's containers: distroboxes (by name, with their image and whether they are running) and podman/docker containers, including any that exited because they ran out of memory, plus how much disk the images use. Use for 'what distroboxes do I have', 'is my container running', 'why did my container die'. The podman details use the 'containers-sense-enabled' switch. Read-only.

train.say: System language and date, number and money formats.
train.positives_desc: set_locale: Report the system language and regional formats, list the locales available on this machine, or change one: the system language, or the date format (British day/month or American month/day order), number format (decimal comma or point), money, measurement or paper size (e.g. what='dates', locale='en_GB.UTF-8'). Takes effect at the next login. Changing requires the 'locale-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, locale, what)

negatives.desc: convert_currency: Convert an amount of money between currencies (rupees, dollars, euros, pounds, yen, ...) at today's ECB reference rate. Requires the web sense and privacy mode off. (arguments: amount, from_currency, to_currency)
get_datetime: The current date and time here. For the time in another city or country, use get_world_time.

date_math: Date arithmetic: days until a date ('how many days until 25 December'), the date N days/weeks/months from a date ('what date is 45 days from now'), days between two dates, or the weekday of a date. (arguments: operation, date, other_date, amount, unit)
get_world_time: The current time and date in ANOTHER city, country or time zone, e.g. 'what time is it in Tokyo'. For the time here, use get_datetime. (arguments: place)

system_history: What this machine's CPU, disk, memory or paging was doing earlier, from the sysstat accounting records rather than a live reading. Use for 'was this busy last night', 'what was using the disk at lunchtime', 'why was the fan loud earlier'. Says plainly when no history has been recorded, because that is not the same as the machine having been idle. Read-only. (arguments: topic)

system_info: Describe the machine Chronoa is running on: distribution, kernel, architecture, uptime, load, memory, CPU count, whether this is a desktop session or a container, and the hardware identity (make, model, board, BIOS version).

open_settings: Open the system Settings app at a specific page, e.g. 'wifi', 'bluetooth', 'display', 'sound', 'power', 'privacy', 'keyboard', 'mouse', 'touchpad', 'printers', 'users', 'about', 'date_time', 'region', 'notifications', 'background', 'accessibility'. GNOME and KDE Plasma. Use open_application for Settings without a page. (arguments: page)

train.say: Press ctrl-alt-f2 in the virtual machine.
train.positives_desc: vm: Run a virtual machine with QEMU and drive it like a browser: launch it with a visible window on the desktop and a QMP control socket beside it, photograph its screen, send key combinations, type text into it, move and click its pointer (percentages of its screen), check its power state, and stop it. Requires the 'vm-control-enabled' consent key, off by default. Listing the VMs already running is `list_vms` (virsh) or this skill's list action; this one starts and drives them. (arguments: action, name, memory_mb, iso, disk, display, firmware, tpm, keys, text, x, y, button)

negatives.desc: ui_elements: Use another app's controls by what they are, through the accessibility tree. apps: which apps are reachable. inspect: list a window's buttons, fields, menus and labels with ids (app = its name; query narrows by text). press: activate an element by id (a button, checkbox, link, menu item). set_text: put text in a field by id. read: an element's text or value. menu: open a menu path like 'File > Export'. drive: one turn of driving - give an action and a control number and the reply is the app's new state in the same short numbered form, which is what a small model can act on. act: click, type or key an app by name or position, with a visible cursor. state: the numbered controls an app is showing. Works on a container's app and on this desktop's own apps alike. Requires 'input-control-enabled'; drive start also runs a container, so it needs 'container-control-enabled' as well. (arguments: action, app, id, text, query, path, do, how, number, image, keys, x, y)

press_key: Press a key or key combination in the focused window, e.g. 'Return', 'Escape', 'Tab' or 'ctrl+shift+t'. This sends a key, not text - use type_text to type a string. Requires the 'input-control-enabled' consent key. X11 only. (arguments: key, repeat)

browse: Open a website and do things on it for the person: find information, fill in forms, click through. Drive a web browser: navigate, read the page's text (get_text), click, type, select options, scroll, move through history, take screenshots and wait for conditions. While Chronoa's window is open this is the in-app browser the user can watch: there it opens only http(s) pages the egress policy allows, and key, hover, drag, upload_file, tabs and evaluate are not available. Otherwise it is a headless Chromium with all actions. Requires the web sense to be enabled and privacy mode to be off. (arguments: action, url, selector, text, key, value, label, files, x, y, to_x, to_y, to_selector, delta_x, delta_y, steps, repeat, tab_id, path, wait_for, timeout, settle)

phone_remote: Press keys on the paired phone as a Bluetooth keyboard: 'press' the camera 'shutter' (takes a photo in the camera app), play_pause, next, previous, volume_up/down, mute; or 'type' text into whatever field is focused on the phone. The phone must have paired 'Chronoa Remote'. Requires the 'phone-remote-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, key, text)

machine_capabilities: Report what this machine can actually do: which of the commands Chronoa knows how to use are really present, which Python modules import here, and which services are enabled. Asks the live machine rather than reading the shipped inventory, which describes the image it was built from and not necessarily this one. Use it before offering to convert a file, edit an image, read a document or capture audio, to find out whether that is even possible here.

list_vms: List the virtual machines defined with libvirt - both your own (GNOME Boxes) and the system-wide ones (virt-manager) - and whether each is running, paused or shut off. Use for 'what VMs do I have', 'is my Windows VM running'. Read-only.

ir_remote: Send and receive infrared remote-control codes, and build or read the pulse-space timings themselves. 'devices': is there IR hardware here (most machines have none, and that is a true answer). 'encode': turn an address and command into the NEC or RC-6 timings that would carry them. 'decode': turn timings into a code. 'send': transmit a code through an IR device. 'receive': capture a button press and decode it. Needs the 'ir-remote-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, protocol, address, command, timings, seconds)

train.say: Push this branch to origin.
train.positives_desc: git_push: Push a branch to a named remote. Requires the 'git-push-enabled' consent key, and asks before every push. The remote must be one the repository already has, and must be named - there is no default and no 'push everything'. Force-pushing is refused. (arguments: remote, branch, set_upstream, path)

negatives.desc: git_branch: Create a branch in a git repository and switch to it, or switch to a branch that already exists. Requires the 'git-write-enabled' consent key. (arguments: name, path)

android_device: An Android phone connected with USB debugging (adb). devices: which are connected; info: model, Android version, battery, storage; screenshot: save the phone's screen as a PNG; apps: installed apps (query filters); push: copy a file to the phone (to, default /sdcard/Download); pull: copy a file from the phone; open_url: open a web link on the phone. Requires 'phone-control-enabled'. (arguments: action, serial, path, to, url, query, output)

maps: OpenStreetMap maps: find where a place is ('find'), driving/walking/cycling directions ('directions') or just distance and time ('travel_time') between places, the nearest kind of place such as petrol pump, hotel, ATM or hospital ('nearby'), or open a place or route on the map in the browser ('open'). Times are typical, without live traffic. With no origin, 'here' is this computer's location. Requires the web sense and privacy mode off; 'here' also needs the location sense. (arguments: action, place, destination, origin, mode, what, near, limit)

bluetooth_gatt: Read what a paired Bluetooth Low Energy device says about itself - a watch's or headset's battery, a heart-rate strap's live reading, which services a band offers. 'list': every paired device and whether it speaks this protocol. 'services': what one exposes. 'read': one stored value. 'listen': a live reading of something the device only pushes, e.g. heart rate - 'nothing arrived' is the truthful answer when the device is not measuring. Speakers, headphones and car stereios are older Bluetooth and expose nothing here, which is a true answer, not a failure; wearables, bands, straps, smart tags and thermometers answer. Needs 'bluetooth-gatt-enabled' and the device must be connected. (arguments: action, device, seconds, characteristic)

git_inspect: Report a git working tree: what has changed and is not committed, the diff of those changes, recent commits, or the current branch and how far it is from its upstream; also the stashed work and the reflog (the record that survives rebases and amends). Reports UNKNOWN - never 'clean tree' - when git is missing, the folder is not a repository, or git fails. Requires the 'git-sense-enabled' consent key. (arguments: path, subcommand, revision, since, context_lines)

git_commit: Commit the files you name in a git repository, with a message. Only the paths given are staged - nothing is swept up from the rest of the tree. Requires the 'git-write-enabled' consent key. Pushing is a separate skill: that publishes. (arguments: files, message, path)

vcs_status: What state a checkout is in, for git, subversion or mercurial: which version control system it belongs to, the branch or revision, the repository it points at, and what has changed. Use when the answer might not be git - 'what is this folder's state', 'which repository is this', 'what changed in my checkout'. Read-only; runs nothing that modifies a repository. (arguments: path)

train.say: Make or extract an archive.
train.positives_desc: create_archive: Create a zip or tar.gz archive from files or folders, or list or safely extract an existing one. Refuses archives whose entries would escape the destination. (arguments: action, source, destination, format)

negatives.desc: extract_archive: Unpack a .tar/.tar.gz/.tgz/.zip archive, or any format 7z reads (.7z, .rar, .cab ...), into a directory. Every member is checked first and the archive is refused whole if any entry would be written outside the destination or is a link, a device or a FIFO. Will not overwrite existing files unless asked. (arguments: archive, destination, overwrite)

list_archive: List what is inside an archive - .tar, .tar.gz, .zip, .7z, .rar or .cab - without extracting anything. Use for 'what's in this archive', 'does this tarball contain what I need'. Names any member that extraction would refuse because it points outside the destination, which is how a malicious archive is recognised before it is opened. Reads only; writes nothing. (arguments: path)

pdf_pages: Work with PDF pages without re-rendering them: 'info' (page count), 'merge' several PDFs into one (paths, in order), 'split' a PDF into one file per page (into a folder), or 'extract' some pages (e.g. '1-3,7') into a new PDF. Always writes new files; never overwrites an existing one or changes the originals. No rotation. (arguments: action, path, paths, pages, output)

space_by_type: Break disk usage down by kind of file - video, audio, image, document, archive, code and so on - across all directories, rather than per directory. Use for 'what is eating my disk', 'is it the photos or the documents', 'what takes up the space in here'. Names the largest category, and reports files whose type it could not tell as a visible `other` bucket rather than dropping them. Read-only. (arguments: path)

web_search: Look something up on the web and return what the pages actually say: facts, prices, how-tos, anything no more specific tool covers. Give a search query, a specific URL, or both. For a scholarly question - a paper, a preprint, prior work, 'what does the research say' - set source=arxiv and it searches the arXiv preprint archive instead of the web. For news headlines use news; to click, fill in or book something on a site use browse. Requires the web sense to be enabled and privacy mode to be off. (arguments: query, url, source)

train.say: Keep your own notes: add, list, search and remove.
train.positives_desc: notes: Keep your own notes in a plain list stored on this machine: 'add' one from 'text', 'list' them, 'search' by text or id, 'remove' one by 'id'. Never sent to a model. For what the assistant itself believes and uses in its replies, use remember_fact instead. (arguments: action, text, query, id)

negatives.desc: search_my_files: Search your own files by meaning - documents, notes, code - in a directory you choose, or your home if you name none. 'search': what matches a few words. 'reindex': read the directory and build or refresh the index (needed before the first search). 'status': what would be indexed and whether this machine can search by meaning. Needs the 'file-index-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, query, path, limit)

todo_list: Keep a list of tasks that survives between turns and restarts: add an item, change its status, mark what it is blocked by, or list what is outstanding. Use this to track a multi-step job rather than holding it in the conversation. Requires the 'todo-list-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, id, content, status, blocked_by)

reminders: A dated list of reminders you can keep coming back to: add one, list what is still due, mark one done, or remove one. Optionally with a due time in words, e.g. 'tomorrow 9am' or 'in 3 hours'. (arguments: action, number, text, due)

search_documents: Search inside the user's files by their contents, using the desktop's own search index (LocalSearch on GNOME, Baloo on Plasma). Requires the 'document-search-enabled' consent key. (arguments: query, kind, limit)

conversations: The user's saved Chronoa conversations. list: recent ones; search: find what was said in earlier conversations (query); open: continue one (which = title or id); new: start a fresh one; rename (which, title); copy: duplicate one to try another way, optionally keeping only its first keep_turns user messages; export: save one as Markdown (path); delete: remove one permanently (needs 'file-delete-enabled'). (arguments: action, which, query, title, path, keep_turns)

manage_triggers: Arm, list, or remove automatic rules that run a Chronoa action when a perception matches - for example, notify when the battery sense reports low. A rule names one already-whitelisted skill; it cannot run an arbitrary command or an LLM-authored prompt. Listing needs no permission; arming or disarming requires the 'trigger-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, name, sense, match_mode, substring, keywords, actuator, arguments, cooldown_seconds, event_type, source, params, ask_first, retry_policy, debounce_seconds)

search_file_contents: Search inside text files under a directory for a literal string, and report which files contain it and on which lines. Skips binary files and very large files, and says how many it skipped. (arguments: text, path, file_pattern, case_sensitive, max_matches)

train.say: What it perceives.
train.positives_desc: list_percepts: Show what Chronoa is currently perceiving - every fact held about this machine and the user right now, with its age, what expires it, and whether it would be included in the next reply. Use this to check what the assistant actually knows rather than what it says. (arguments: sense_filter, include_expired)

train.say: Search inside files.
train.positives_desc: search_file_contents: Search inside text files under a directory for a literal string, and report which files contain it and on which lines. Skips binary files and very large files, and says how many it skipped. (arguments: text, path, file_pattern, case_sensitive, max_matches)

negatives.desc: search_my_files: Search your own files by meaning - documents, notes, code - in a directory you choose, or your home if you name none. 'search': what matches a few words. 'reindex': read the directory and build or refresh the index (needed before the first search). 'status': what would be indexed and whether this machine can search by meaning. Needs the 'file-index-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, query, path, limit)

search_documents: Search inside the user's files by their contents, using the desktop's own search index (LocalSearch on GNOME, Baloo on Plasma). Requires the 'document-search-enabled' consent key. (arguments: query, kind, limit)

cloud_files: See what is in this machine's configured cloud storage remotes - which remotes rclone knows, how many objects and bytes each holds, and what is at the top level of one. Use for 'what is in my cloud drive', 'is anything in the bucket', 'how big is my remote'. Read-only: it never copies, syncs or deletes anything. A machine with no remotes says so, because that means there is nowhere off-machine for anything to go. (arguments: remote, path)

duplicate_files: Find files with identical content under a directory, and how much space the copies waste. Use for 'why is my disk full', 'are there duplicates in my Downloads', 'where is my space going'. Reports verified groups only - same size is evidence, a matching hash is proof - and never marks one copy as the original. Read-only: it hashes and lists, and deletes nothing. (arguments: path, limit)

files_by_name: Find every file with a given name under a directory, with sizes and modification dates, so you can see whether they are copies. Use for 'where are all my report.docx', 'how many copies of this do I have', 'which is the newest'. Reports the newest and whether the sizes agree, and does NOT claim the contents match - duplicate_files answers that. Deletes nothing. (arguments: name, path, case_sensitive)

find_files: Find files and folders by name under a directory, using a wildcard pattern such as '*.log' or 'report*'. Matches on the name only and never opens the files. To see what is in one folder, use list_directory. (arguments: pattern, path, include_hidden, max_results)

stale_files: Find files that are both large and untouched for a long time - the deletion candidates a disk-usage answer only gestures at. Use for 'what can I delete', 'what is safe to clean up', 'what in here is old and big'. Reports candidates only: it claims nothing is safe to delete, removes nothing, and says that an untouched timestamp is not proof a file is unused. Read-only. (arguments: path, older_than_days, limit)

train.say: Say what is charging this machine, and how fast.
train.positives_desc: charger_info: Report what is powering this machine: on battery or plugged in, AC adapter or USB-C, whether USB Power Delivery is in use, and the charger's wattage when the firmware reports it, plus battery charge and rate.

negatives.desc: network_activity: Report what this machine's network is doing right now, per program: which processes are sending and receiving, and how fast each interface is moving. Use for 'what is using my bandwidth', 'why is the network slow', 'what is uploading', 'is something downloading right now'. Interface rates come from /proc/net/dev and always work; per-program rates need nethogs and can only name programs this user owns. Says which half it could not measure and why, and reports an unattributed socket as unattributed rather than guessing at a program. Read-only; nothing is changed or blocked.

manage_triggers: Arm, list, or remove automatic rules that run a Chronoa action when a perception matches - for example, notify when the battery sense reports low. A rule names one already-whitelisted skill; it cannot run an arbitrary command or an LLM-authored prompt. Listing needs no permission; arming or disarming requires the 'trigger-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, name, sense, match_mode, substring, keywords, actuator, arguments, cooldown_seconds, event_type, source, params, ask_first, retry_policy, debounce_seconds)

bandwidth_to_host: Measure how fast this machine can send data to another machine over the network, using a controlled iperf3 transfer. Use for 'why is my NAS slow', 'how fast is my network to the server', 'is the bottleneck the network or the disk'. Needs iperf3 running on the other machine - ask for loopback to measure this machine against itself. Read-only: it transfers data and writes nothing. (arguments: host, port, seconds)

machine_capabilities: Report what this machine can actually do: which of the commands Chronoa knows how to use are really present, which Python modules import here, and which services are enabled. Asks the live machine rather than reading the shipped inventory, which describes the image it was built from and not necessarily this one. Use it before offering to convert a file, edit an image, read a document or capture audio, to find out whether that is even possible here.
get_battery_status: Get the current battery charge percentage and charging state.

edit_video: Edit a video and save the result as a new file next to it (never overwriting the original): trim between times, resize to a width, rotate, mute or keep only the audio, or change the speed. End times accept seconds ('95'), or 'MM:SS' / 'HH:MM:SS'. (arguments: path, start, end, width, rotate, mute, audio_only, speed, output)

speed_test: Measure this internet connection: latency, download speed and upload speed, against Cloudflare's speed-test servers. Moves real data (default 10 MB down, 2 MB up), so it requires the 'speed-test-enabled' consent key and privacy mode off. Use for 'how fast is my internet', 'is my connection slow'. (arguments: download_mb, upload_mb)

temperatures: Current CPU, GPU, disk and board temperatures, fan speeds and fan control, read from the kernel's hardware sensors. Use for 'is my laptop overheating', 'how hot is the CPU', 'how fast is the fan'. Uses the 'hwmon-sense-enabled' switch. Read-only.

train.say: Press buttons, fill fields and open menus in other apps.
train.positives_desc: ui_elements: Use another app's controls by what they are, through the accessibility tree. apps: which apps are reachable. inspect: list a window's buttons, fields, menus and labels with ids (app = its name; query narrows by text). press: activate an element by id (a button, checkbox, link, menu item). set_text: put text in a field by id. read: an element's text or value. menu: open a menu path like 'File > Export'. drive: one turn of driving - give an action and a control number and the reply is the app's new state in the same short numbered form, which is what a small model can act on. act: click, type or key an app by name or position, with a visible cursor. state: the numbered controls an app is showing. Works on a container's app and on this desktop's own apps alike. Requires 'input-control-enabled'; drive start also runs a container, so it needs 'container-control-enabled' as well. (arguments: action, app, id, text, query, path, do, how, number, image, keys, x, y)

negatives.desc: phone_remote: Press keys on the paired phone as a Bluetooth keyboard: 'press' the camera 'shutter' (takes a photo in the camera app), play_pause, next, previous, volume_up/down, mute; or 'type' text into whatever field is focused on the phone. The phone must have paired 'Chronoa Remote'. Requires the 'phone-remote-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, key, text)

Drive a web browser: navigate, read the page's text (get_text), click, type, select options, scroll, move through history, take screenshots and wait for conditions. Otherwise it is a headless Chromium with all actions. Requires the web sense to be enabled and privacy mode to be off. (arguments: action, url, selector, text, key, value, label, files, x, y, to_x, to_y, to_selector, delta_x, delta_y, steps, repeat, tab_id, path, wait_for, timeout, settle)

ir_remote: Send and receive infrared remote-control codes, and build or read the pulse-space timings themselves. 'devices': is there IR hardware here (most machines have none, and that is a true answer). 'encode': turn an address and command into the NEC or RC-6 timings that would carry them. 'decode': turn timings into a code. 'send': transmit a code through an IR device. 'receive': capture a button press and decode it. Needs the 'ir-remote-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, protocol, address, command, timings, seconds)

press_key: Press a key or key combination in the focused window, e.g. 'Return', 'Escape', 'Tab' or 'ctrl+shift+t'. This sends a key, not text - use type_text to type a string. Requires the 'input-control-enabled' consent key. X11 only. (arguments: key, repeat)

default_apps: Show or change which application opens a kind of file - by MIME type ('application/pdf'), extension ('.pdf', 'mp4') or an example file - or the default web browser (target 'browser'). Use for 'what opens PDFs', 'make VLC open my videos', 'set Firefox as my default browser'. Changing a default requires the 'default-apps-enabled' consent key; showing one does not. (arguments: target, action, app)

list_apps: List the applications installed on this machine, optionally filtered by a search term, so a request to open something can be answered with what actually exists rather than a guess. (arguments: search)

android_device: An Android phone connected with USB debugging (adb). devices: which are connected; info: model, Android version, battery, storage; screenshot: save the phone's screen as a PNG; apps: installed apps (query filters); push: copy a file to the phone (to, default /sdcard/Download); pull: copy a file from the phone; open_url: open a web link on the phone. Requires 'phone-control-enabled'. (arguments: action, serial, path, to, url, query, output)

train.say: Inspect a TLS certificate.
train.positives_desc: tls_certificate: Read a website's TLS certificate: when it expires, who issued it, and which hostnames it covers. Use for 'when does this site's certificate expire' or 'why is HTTPS failing on this'. (arguments: host, port)

negatives.desc: git_inspect: Report a git working tree: what has changed and is not committed, the diff of those changes, recent commits, or the current branch and how far it is from its upstream; also the stashed work and the reflog (the record that survives rebases and amends). Reports UNKNOWN - never 'clean tree' - when git is missing, the folder is not a repository, or git fails. Requires the 'git-sense-enabled' consent key. (arguments: path, subcommand, revision, since, context_lines)

inspect_binary: What a compiled program is and whether it can run here: 32- or 64-bit, which CPU architecture, whether it is an executable or a shared library, the dynamic loader it needs, and every shared library it requires - naming any that are missing from this machine, which is what 'error while loading shared libraries' means. Answers 'what architecture is this', 'what is this file', 'why won't this program start'. Reads only the file; it is never executed and never run with root. (arguments: path)

ui_elements: Use another app's controls by what they are, through the accessibility tree. apps: which apps are reachable. inspect: list a window's buttons, fields, menus and labels with ids (app = its name; query narrows by text). press: activate an element by id (a button, checkbox, link, menu item). set_text: put text in a field by id. read: an element's text or value. menu: open a menu path like 'File > Export'. drive: one turn of driving - give an action and a control number and the reply is the app's new state in the same short numbered form, which is what a small model can act on. act: click, type or key an app by name or position, with a visible cursor. state: the numbered controls an app is showing. Works on a container's app and on this desktop's own apps alike. Requires 'input-control-enabled'; drive start also runs a container, so it needs 'container-control-enabled' as well. (arguments: action, app, id, text, query, path, do, how, number, image, keys, x, y)

dissect_traffic: Capture traffic on an interface and dissect it into protocol fields with tshark, Wireshark's command-line engine: which protocols are actually on the wire, and for a filter, the specific fields - TLS handshake type and SNI, DNS query names, HTTP host. This is the companion to capture_packets: that one reads packets as they cross, this one says what they are. Filters use the same grammar as both tools. Reads packet contents, so it needs the same permission as capture_packets. Writes nothing to disk. (arguments: interface, filter, packets, seconds)

dns_lookup: Look a hostname or address up in DNS and report what came back: the addresses, or the mail servers, name servers, TXT records, certificate records or other records a name publishes, and whether the answer is DNSSEC-signed and valid. Distinguishes 'this name does not exist' from 'the resolver did not answer', because those have different fixes. Obeys privacy mode, since the query goes to a resolver outside this machine. Read-only. (arguments: name, type)

binary_hardening: Report whether a binary is hardened: PIE, RELRO, full RELRO (BIND_NOW), stack canary and no-execute stack, each with what it stops. Use for 'is /path/to/this safe to run', 'is this binary hardened', 'does this have a stack canary', 'is this ASLR enabled'. Works on executables and shared libraries alike, and says 'not applicable' where a property genuinely has no answer rather than reporting it as missing. Read-only; nothing is loaded or written. (arguments: path)

train.say: Make a slideshow or colour clip.
train.positives_desc: create_video: Create a video: a slideshow from a list of pictures (each shown for a few seconds), or a simple clip of a colour for a duration. Writes a new .mp4 next to the inputs; never overwrites. (arguments: images, seconds, color, duration, width)

negatives.desc: photo_video: Blur or pixelate faces, blur or remove the background, or find people and objects in a photo or video. Works by what is in it, on this computer. identify: find faces and everyday objects (people, cars, dogs, cups...); effect: blur_faces, pixelate_faces, blur_background or remove_background, saved as a new file (videos keep their sound); keyframes: save the moments a video changes; describe: say what happens in a video. For a look like sepia or sketch, or resizing and converting, use edit_image or convert_media. (arguments: action, path, effect, subject, labelled_copy)

take_photo: Take a photo or selfie with the webcam and save it to the Pictures folder, optionally after a countdown in seconds (0-30). Requires the vision/camera consent. Not for screenshots (use screenshot) or video (use capture_video). (arguments: countdown, path, device, infrared)

photo_metadata: Read a photo's embedded EXIF metadata: the camera and lens, the date and time it was taken, exposure, aperture, ISO, focal length, and the GPS location if one is recorded. Use for 'when was this photo taken', 'does this picture contain my location', 'which camera took it'. JPEG and TIFF. Read-only; the file is not changed. (arguments: path)

photos: Find the user's photos by what is in them or written on them, or when they were taken. search: query like 'receipt hardware shop', 'dog on the beach', 'december 2025'; index: update the index of the Pictures folder (a batch at a time); status: how much is indexed. (arguments: action, query, captions)

capture_video: Record a short video from the camera (webcam), e.g. '/dev/video0', for a few seconds. Requires the vision/camera consent. Writes a new .mp4; no camera means a clear refusal. (arguments: device, seconds, infrared)

edit_video: Edit a video and save the result as a new file next to it (never overwriting the original): trim between times, resize to a width, rotate, mute or keep only the audio, or change the speed. End times accept seconds ('95'), or 'MM:SS' / 'HH:MM:SS'. (arguments: path, start, end, width, rotate, mute, audio_only, speed, output)

read_video: Read a video's basics out loud (for subtitles or what was said use recording): how long it is, its resolution, its video codec, whether it has audio, and its bitrate. Add keyframes=true to also save the moments the image changes. The original is never modified. (arguments: path, keyframes)

train.say: Internet speed.
train.positives_desc: speed_test: Measure this internet connection: latency, download speed and upload speed, against Cloudflare's speed-test servers. Moves real data (default 10 MB down, 2 MB up), so it requires the 'speed-test-enabled' consent key and privacy mode off. Use for 'how fast is my internet', 'is my connection slow'. (arguments: download_mb, upload_mb)

Give a search query, a specific URL, or both. For a scholarly question - a paper, a preprint, prior work, 'what does the research say' - set source=arxiv and it searches the arXiv preprint archive instead of the web. For news headlines use news; to click, fill in or book something on a site use browse. Requires the web sense to be enabled and privacy mode to be off. (arguments: query, url, source)
check_internet: Check whether the internet is working and, if not, which step fails: network connection, router, internet, DNS, or websites. Also reports the delay to the router and to the internet.

search_documents: Search inside the user's files by their contents, using the desktop's own search index (LocalSearch on GNOME, Baloo on Plasma). Requires the 'document-search-enabled' consent key. (arguments: query, kind, limit)

search_file_contents: Search inside text files under a directory for a literal string, and report which files contain it and on which lines. Skips binary files and very large files, and says how many it skipped. (arguments: text, path, file_pattern, case_sensitive, max_matches)

search_my_files: Search your own files by meaning - documents, notes, code - in a directory you choose, or your home if you name none. 'search': what matches a few words. 'reindex': read the directory and build or refresh the index (needed before the first search). 'status': what would be indexed and whether this machine can search by meaning. Needs the 'file-index-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, query, path, limit)
my_ip_address: This computer's IP addresses: local (LAN) addresses per network interface, and the public internet address when the web sense is on.

news: News headlines only (title, source, age), from Google News (or BBC) RSS feeds - not facts or what a page says, which is web_search. With no topic: the top stories. A topic can be a section - world, business, tech, science, health, sports, entertainment - or anything to search for, e.g. 'ISRO'. Requires the web sense to be enabled and privacy mode to be off. (arguments: topic, source, limit)

train.say: Change one exact piece of text.
train.positives_desc: edit_file: Replace one exact piece of text in one named file. The text to replace must appear exactly once, or nothing is written - the count and line numbers are reported instead of a guess being made. Use this to change a specific line; use find_and_replace to change a string across many files. Requires the 'file-edit-enabled' consent key. (arguments: path, old_string, new_string, preview, replace_all)

negatives.desc: translate_text: Translate text into another language, using a local translation tool when one is installed and a web service otherwise. The reply says which was used, because one sends your text to a third party. (arguments: text, to_language, from_language)

undo_last_change: Put a file back the way Chronoa last found it, by restoring the content recorded just before Chronoa's own last edit to it. Undoes Chronoa's recent writes only - NOT git history, NOT changes you made in an editor or a shell, and only while a recorded pre-image is still held. Requires the 'file-edit-enabled' consent key. (arguments: path, list, steps)

phone: The user's paired phone via GSConnect/KDE Connect: status (reachable, battery), ring it to find it, ping it, share a file or link to it; read text messages ('messages': latest, from a contact, or unread only); send a text message ('send': to a contact name or number, or omit contact to reply to the latest conversation) with exactly the text given - draft it first; or 'call' a contact or number (opens the phone's dialer). The user confirms every message and call before it goes. Requires the 'phone-control-enabled' consent key; reading needs 'phone-messages-read-enabled', sending and calling 'phone-messages-send-enabled'. (arguments: action, device, target, contact, text, unread_only, limit)

alarm: Alarm clock: set an alarm at a time of day (once, or repeating daily/weekdays/weekends/chosen days), list alarms, say when the next one is, change one's time or label, snooze the one that just rang, or delete one. Examples: 'set an alarm for 7am', 'alarm for 6:30 on weekdays', 'when is my next alarm?', 'change my 7am alarm to 7:30', 'snooze', 'delete the 7am alarm'. Times may be words ('7am', '7:30 pm', 'tomorrow 6:45'). It rings with a notification and the alarm sound even if the assistant is closed; it is held by systemd --user, so a reboot drops it until alarms are next listed, which re-arms it. (arguments: action, time, label, repeat, id, new_time, new_label, minutes)

calendar_edit: Change the user's calendar: 'create' adds an event to the default calendar (title, start, optional duration or end, location); 'move' reschedules an event found by its current time and/or title to new_start; 'cancel' deletes one. Times in words: 'tomorrow 3pm', 'friday 5 pm', '2026-10-09 14:00'. Move and cancel ask the person to confirm. Ambiguous matches are refused with the candidates. Requires the 'calendar-write-enabled' consent key (move/cancel also 'calendar-read-enabled'). No invitations are sent. (arguments: action, title, start, duration, end, new_start, location, notes)
encode_text: Encode or decode text: base64, url (percent-encoding), hex, binary, rot13, morse. (arguments: text, scheme, direction)
type_text: Type text at the currently focused window. Requires the 'input-control-enabled' consent key (separate from the vision sense) to be enabled. (arguments: text)

train.say: what time is it in Tokyo
train.positives_desc: get_world_time: The current time and date in ANOTHER city, country or time zone, e.g. 'what time is it in Tokyo'. For the time here, use get_datetime. (arguments: place)

negatives.desc: get_datetime: The current date and time here. For the time in another city or country, use get_world_time.

alarm: Alarm clock: set an alarm at a time of day (once, or repeating daily/weekdays/weekends/chosen days), list alarms, say when the next one is, change one's time or label, snooze the one that just rang, or delete one. Examples: 'set an alarm for 7am', 'alarm for 6:30 on weekdays', 'when is my next alarm?', 'change my 7am alarm to 7:30', 'snooze', 'delete the 7am alarm'. (arguments: action, time, label, repeat, id, new_time, new_label, minutes)

maps: OpenStreetMap maps: find where a place is ('find'), driving/walking/cycling directions ('directions') or just distance and time ('travel_time') between places, the nearest kind of place such as petrol pump, hotel, ATM or hospital ('nearby'), or open a place or route on the map in the browser ('open'). Times are typical, without live traffic. With no origin, 'here' is this computer's location. Requires the web sense and privacy mode off; 'here' also needs the location sense. (arguments: action, place, destination, origin, mode, what, near, limit)

watch: Your MoYoung/Da Fit smartwatch: 'summary' (steps, distance, calories for 3 days, last night's sleep stages, today's stress, workouts), 'measure' a heart rate, blood oxygen or blood pressure on the wrist (takes up to a minute), read 'settings', 'set' one (step_goal, time_format 12h/24h, units metric/imperial, raise_to_wake, sedentary_reminder, other_app_notifications, power_saving, heart_rate_auto_interval, do_not_disturb '22:00-07:00'), 'sync_time', 'notify' (show a message on the watch), or set the 'profile' (height, weight, age, gender - weight is never measured by the watch). Requires the 'bluetooth-gatt-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, device, what, setting, value, sender, text, kind, height_cm, weight_kg, age, gender)

desktop_setting: Read or change one desktop setting from a fixed list: animations (window and menu animations); cursor_size (mouse pointer size in pixels (24 is normal; 32, 48, 64 are larger)); single_click (open files and folders with a single click); clock_24h (show the top-bar clock in 24-hour format); clock_seconds (show seconds in the top-bar clock); battery_percentage (show the battery percentage in the top bar); hot_corner (open the overview when the pointer hits the top-left corner); natural_scroll (touchpad natural (reverse) scrolling); tap_to_click (tap the touchpad to click). Changing requires the 'appearance-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: setting, value)

boot_report: How the last boot went: total boot time split into firmware, loader, kernel and userspace, the services that took longest to start, when the machine booted and whether it shut down cleanly before, and which EFI entry the firmware will boot by default. Use for 'why does it boot slowly', 'did it crash last time'. Boot history uses the 'boots-sense-enabled' switch. Read-only. (arguments: top)

calculate: Evaluate arithmetic and percentages ('15% of 2400'), or convert between units. Handles the four operations, powers, parentheses, factorial, permutations and combinations (perm/nPr, comb/nCr), gcd, lcm, sqrt, exp, log, ln, trig and inverse trig, and pi/e/tau - exact for whole numbers. For algebra with variables, derivatives, integrals, limits or equations, use solve_math. Converts length, mass, volume, time, data, pressure, frequency, power, energy and temperature, in the units a person actually meets - say '200 km to miles' or '70kg in lb'. Runs entirely on this machine with no network call. Refuses to guess: a percentage needs a number to apply to, and converting between quantities that measure different things is an error rather than a number. (arguments: expression)

train.say: read the file ~/notes/todo.txt
train.positives_desc: read_text_file: Read a text file and return its contents, optionally a range of lines. Use this to see what a file actually says. (arguments: path, start_line, max_lines)

negatives.desc: todo_list: Keep a list of tasks that survives between turns and restarts: add an item, change its status, mark what it is blocked by, or list what is outstanding. Use this to track a multi-step job rather than holding it in the conversation. Requires the 'todo-list-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, id, content, status, blocked_by)

file_locks: Show who holds a file lock, and on what - the answer to "why won't this file save" and "why did my write fail with EAGAIN". A WRITE lock blocks another writer; a READ lock is shared and usually harmless. Use for 'who has this file locked', 'what is holding a lock', 'why can't I write this file', 'is this file locked'. Give a path to check one file; omit it for every lock on the machine. Reads the kernel's own lock table (/proc/locks), so it needs no binary and no privilege. Read-only; nothing is polled, changed or broken. (arguments: path)

notes: Keep your own notes in a plain list stored on this machine: 'add' one from 'text', 'list' them, 'search' by text or id, 'remove' one by 'id'. Never sent to a model. For what the assistant itself believes and uses in its replies, use remember_fact instead. (arguments: action, text, query, id)
convert_document: Convert a document between markdown, plain text, and HTML. Writes a new file next to the original; never overwrites. (arguments: path, to)
create_document: Create a document from a title and body: a markdown file, a plain text file, or an HTML page. Writes a new file; never overwrites. (arguments: title, body, format, path)

meeting: Hold a meeting: record the microphone for as long as it takes, transcribe it with who said what, and write notes. 'record': start now and run for the given number of minutes (default 120, the ceiling). 'notes': write notes from a recording that already exists. 'status': what a meeting would do on this machine. The recording, the transcript and the notes are all written on this computer and nothing leaves it. Needs the 'meeting-enabled' consent key, which is off by default - this holds the microphone for possibly hours, with other people speaking. (arguments: action, minutes, path)

search_my_files: Search your own files by meaning - documents, notes, code - in a directory you choose, or your home if you name none. 'search': what matches a few words. 'reindex': read the directory and build or refresh the index (needed before the first search). 'status': what would be indexed and whether this machine can search by meaning. Needs the 'file-index-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, query, path, limit)

train.say: Why booting is slow, and whether it shut down cleanly.
train.positives_desc: boot_report: How the last boot went: total boot time split into firmware, loader, kernel and userspace, the services that took longest to start, when the machine booted and whether it shut down cleanly before, and which EFI entry the firmware will boot by default. Use for 'why does it boot slowly', 'did it crash last time'. Boot history uses the 'boots-sense-enabled' switch. Read-only. (arguments: top)

negatives.desc: power_action: Suspend (sleep), hibernate, restart or shut down this computer, or cancel a scheduled restart/shutdown. Restart and shutdown happen after one minute and can be cancelled. Requires the 'power-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action)
check_internet: Check whether the internet is working and, if not, which step fails: network connection, router, internet, DNS, or websites. Also reports the delay to the router and to the internet.

set_power_profile: Switch the machine between its power profiles - typically power-saver, balanced and performance - and report which one is active now. The profile list is read from the machine rather than assumed, because which profiles exist depends on the CPU driver: switching to one the machine does not have is refused with the valid names listed. Changes the CPU and platform power behaviour, not a per-application setting. (arguments: profile)

trace_route: Trace the network path to a host: every router along the way, how much of the traffic each one dropped, and how many milliseconds it took. Use when something specific is slow or unreachable, which is different from whether the internet works at all. (arguments: host, probes)

vm: Run a virtual machine with QEMU and drive it like a browser: launch it with a visible window on the desktop and a QMP control socket beside it, photograph its screen, send key combinations, type text into it, move and click its pointer (percentages of its screen), check its power state, and stop it. Requires the 'vm-control-enabled' consent key, off by default. Listing the VMs already running is `list_vms` (virsh) or this skill's list action; this one starts and drives them. (arguments: action, name, memory_mb, iso, disk, display, firmware, tpm, keys, text, x, y, button)

speed_test: Measure this internet connection: latency, download speed and upload speed, against Cloudflare's speed-test servers. Moves real data (default 10 MB down, 2 MB up), so it requires the 'speed-test-enabled' consent key and privacy mode off. Use for 'how fast is my internet', 'is my connection slow'. (arguments: download_mb, upload_mb)

train.say: timer 90 seconds for the eggs
train.positives_desc: set_timer: Set a countdown timer that sends a desktop notification when it finishes; list pending timers, say how much time is left, add or take off time, pause, resume, reset to the original length, and cancel. With one timer pending, 'my timer' needs no id. The countdown is owned by systemd, so it fires even if the assistant is closed. It is refused rather than silently accepted when systemd is unavailable, because a timer recorded as pending that will never fire is the same lie as a camera reported as disabled when it is not. (arguments: action, seconds, label, id)

negatives.desc: scheduled_tasks: What is scheduled to run on this machine: your crontab, the system crontab and /etc/cron.d, and both the system and your systemd timers. Each source is reported separately and one that cannot be read says so, because a machine can have no user crontab and still have nine timers. Reading what the machine has scheduled describes the machine rather than the person's world, so it needs no permission. Nothing is scheduled, changed or removed by asking. (arguments: source)

autostart_entries: Report everything on this machine that starts automatically: the autostart .desktop files in this user's home and /etc/xdg, the enabled systemd user units and timers, and the crontab. Use for 'what starts automatically', 'what runs at login', 'what is scheduled', 'why does this thing keep running', 'what did I set to start on its own'. Honours Hidden, OnlyShowIn and NotShowIn, and says 'cannot tell' rather than guessing when the desktop is unknown - which is the normal state outside a login session. Read-only; nothing is enabled, disabled or changed.

lan_phone: Find phones on the SAME Wi-Fi network, using the KDE Connect protocol directly - so it works without KDE Connect or GSConnect installed. 'devices': what announced itself on this network in the last few seconds (phones, tablets, other computers). 'announce': make this computer findable by a phone's KDE Connect app. 'status': what this computer can and cannot do on the LAN. 'pair': what the pairing half of the protocol is and why it is not here. Needs the 'lan-phone-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, seconds)

desktop_setting: Read or change one desktop setting from a fixed list: animations (window and menu animations); cursor_size (mouse pointer size in pixels (24 is normal; 32, 48, 64 are larger)); single_click (open files and folders with a single click); clock_24h (show the top-bar clock in 24-hour format); clock_seconds (show seconds in the top-bar clock); battery_percentage (show the battery percentage in the top bar); hot_corner (open the overview when the pointer hits the top-left corner); natural_scroll (touchpad natural (reverse) scrolling); tap_to_click (tap the touchpad to click). Changing requires the 'appearance-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: setting, value)

print_file: Print a document file on the default printer, or on a named one. Refuses directories and non-document files. Reports the job as queued, since whether it actually printed is not observable from here. (arguments: path, printer)

print_queue: Show the printers, which one is the default, the print jobs still waiting, and what this machine can print to even when nothing is configured; or cancel a waiting job by its id. Use for 'what's printing', 'why isn't my printer there', 'what can I print to', 'cancel that print'. Cancelling requires the 'print-control-enabled' consent key; listing does not. (arguments: action, job, printer, option)

Use this to track a multi-step job rather than holding it in the conversation. Requires the 'todo-list-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, id, content, status, blocked_by)

train.say: how much disk space is free?
train.positives_desc: disk_usage: Report how full each filesystem is, and optionally which directories under a given path use the most space. Read-only: it never deletes anything. (arguments: path)

negatives.desc: space_by_type: Break disk usage down by kind of file - video, audio, image, document, archive, code and so on - across all directories, rather than per directory. Use for 'what is eating my disk', 'is it the photos or the documents', 'what takes up the space in here'. Names the largest category, and reports files whose type it could not tell as a visible `other` bucket rather than dropping them. Read-only. (arguments: path)

cleanup_apply: Actually free the disk space cleanup_report measured: empty your cache folder, or remove Flatpak runtimes no app uses. Both are recoverable or provably unused. Requires the 'cleanup-enabled' consent key. The system log is not here - that needs root, which Chronoa cannot ask for from inside a tool call. (arguments: target)
cleanup_report: Report what could be cleaned up to free disk space - trash, caches, the system log, unused Flatpak runtimes - with sizes. Reads only; deletes nothing.

disk_activity: How hard this machine's disks are working right now: reads and writes per second, average wait, and how much of each disk's time is spent busy. Answers 'why is my computer slow', 'why is the disk grinding', 'is something writing all the time'. Read-only; nothing is started or stopped.

disk_health: Health of this machine's drives (SMART/NVMe status and wear where it can be read) and whether each mounted filesystem - /, /home and the rest - sits on an encrypted (LUKS) volume. Use for 'is my SSD healthy', 'is my disk encrypted', 'how worn is my drive'. Drive health uses the 'storage-sense-enabled' switch. Read-only.

disk_layout: Show how this machine's disks are partitioned: every physical disk, each partition with its size, filesystem and purpose (EFI, Linux root, /home, LUKS, LVM, swap), and where each one is mounted. Use for 'how is my disk partitioned', 'what partitions are on this machine', 'which partition is my home directory on', 'is my disk GPT or plain', 'what is this LUKS partition for'. Follows the storage sense's consent switch, because it reports the same machine. Read-only; nothing is changed. Loop devices (the immutable snap images) are hidden unless show_hidden is set, and their count is always stated. (arguments: show_hidden)

compression_savings: How much space btrfs compression is saving on this machine: the uncompressed size of the data, how much disk it actually occupies, and which compressor is doing it. Use for 'how much is compression saving me', 'why is my disk less full than the files suggest'. Read-only; nothing is changed.

train.say: Who logged in recently.
train.positives_desc: login_history: Recent logins to this machine: which user, from which terminal or remote address, when they started and how long they lasted, and recent reboots. Use for 'who logged in', 'has anyone used my computer'. Requires the 'sessions-sense-enabled' consent key, because it reports other people's presence. Read-only. (arguments: limit)

negatives.desc: find_recently_modified: List files under a directory whose recorded modification time is within the last N days, newest first. Use this to answer 'what did I change today'. This is a timestamp, so a tool that preserves or sets times (tar, rsync, cp -p) can move an entry without the content changing. (arguments: path, within_days, pattern, limit)

log_files: See which log files under /var/log are largest, whether they are still being written to right now, and whether anything rotates them. Use for 'why is my disk full', 'what is filling up the disk', 'is that log growing'. Also reports logrotate configuration errors, which silently stop a rotation. Read-only: it runs logrotate in debug mode, which rotates nothing. (arguments: limit)

read_logs: Read recent log output from a named system service, or from the kernel when no service is named. Returns the most recent lines first-context-last, and says how much it did not show. (arguments: unit, lines, priority, since)

crash_report: Programs that crashed recently on this machine (core dumps recorded by systemd-coredump): which program, when, and the signal that killed it. Use for 'what crashed', 'why did that app close'. Uses the 'coredumps-sense-enabled' switch. Read-only.

For algebra with variables, derivatives, integrals, limits or equations, use solve_math. Requires the 'cleanup-enabled' consent key. The system log is not here - that needs root, which Chronoa cannot ask for from inside a tool call. (arguments: target)

container: Run containers on this machine with podman (run an image, run a command inside a running container, stop it, read its logs, list what is running, list local images, pull one) and start/stop nspawn machines with machinectl. A container started with display=x11 draws on this desktop, and the ui_elements tool is what drives it by name with a visible cursor; this tool starts it, and stops it. Needs 'container-control-enabled', off by default. (arguments: action, image, name, command, detach, display, share_bus, publish, all, tail)

train.say: Watch the packets crossing an interface.
train.positives_desc: capture_packets: Watch packets crossing one network interface for a few seconds, and report tcpdump's one-line-per-packet summaries: who sent to whom, which protocol, how long, and the TCP flags. This reads packet contents on the wire - it is the one thing in this package that does - so it is gated separately and shows no payload text. Bounded by packet count, seconds and output rows. Read-only: it captures and prints, and changes nothing. (arguments: interface, packets, seconds, filter)

negatives.desc: interface_counters: Report how many bytes and packets each network interface has carried, in each direction, with its error and drop counters, plus the machine's TCP retransmit and error totals. Totals are since each interface came up, and the figures are read from /proc so no daemon needs to be running. Optionally sample twice to get a rate. Read-only. Counts one network namespace: an interface inside a network namespace is not visible here. (arguments: interface, sample_seconds, limit)

watch: Your MoYoung/Da Fit smartwatch: 'summary' (steps, distance, calories for 3 days, last night's sleep stages, today's stress, workouts), 'measure' a heart rate, blood oxygen or blood pressure on the wrist (takes up to a minute), read 'settings', 'set' one (step_goal, time_format 12h/24h, units metric/imperial, raise_to_wake, sedentary_reminder, other_app_notifications, power_saving, heart_rate_auto_interval, do_not_disturb '22:00-07:00'), 'sync_time', 'notify' (show a message on the watch), or set the 'profile' (height, weight, age, gender - weight is never measured by the watch). Requires the 'bluetooth-gatt-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, device, what, setting, value, sender, text, kind, height_cm, weight_kg, age, gender)

dissect_traffic: Capture traffic on an interface and dissect it into protocol fields with tshark, Wireshark's command-line engine: which protocols are actually on the wire, and for a filter, the specific fields - TLS handshake type and SNI, DNS query names, HTTP host. This is the companion to capture_packets: that one reads packets as they cross, this one says what they are. Filters use the same grammar as both tools. Reads packet contents, so it needs the same permission as capture_packets. Writes nothing to disk. (arguments: interface, filter, packets, seconds)

discover_hosts: Find which devices are on this network right now, by asking rather than by reading the cache - so devices that have never talked to this machine are found too. Reports an address and a hardware address for each, and counts devices answering on more than one address. The range is always the private network this machine is on; pass network= for a different private range, and a public one is refused. Connects to nothing it finds and reads no packet contents. Needs raw-socket access, so unprivileged it may report that rather than a partial sweep. (arguments: interface, network)

neighbour_table: Show the neighbour (ARP) table for this machine: which addresses on this link have answered, which have never answered and are holding packets instead of sending them, and which have gone stale. That distinction is the one layer 3 cannot make - an unresolved neighbour and a switched-off host both look like 'no reply', and they have opposite fixes. Read from /proc, so no privileges are needed. One network namespace. (arguments: device)

'list': every paired device and whether it speaks this protocol. 'services': what one exposes. 'read': one stored value. 'listen': a live reading of something the device only pushes, e.g. heart rate - 'nothing arrived' is the truthful answer when the device is not measuring. Speakers, headphones and car stereios are older Bluetooth and expose nothing here, which is a true answer, not a failure; wearables, bands, straps, smart tags and thermometers answer. Needs 'bluetooth-gatt-enabled' and the device must be connected. (arguments: action, device, seconds, characteristic)

Works on devices with the standard Immediate Alert service and on MoYoung (Da Fit) watches; anything else is refused rather than sent an unknown command. The device must be in range. Requires the 'bluetooth-gatt-enabled' consent key. (arguments: device)
