firmware_updates: List firmware updates fwupd knows for this machine's devices (BIOS, SSD, dock, touchpad...) and what each fixes, plus the firmware versions this machine is running. Read-only; nothing is installed.

manage_triggers: Arm, list, or remove automatic rules that run a Chronoa action when a perception matches - for example, notify when the battery sense reports low. A rule names one already-whitelisted skill; it cannot run an arbitrary command or an LLM-authored prompt. Listing needs no permission; arming or disarming requires the 'trigger-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, name, sense, match_mode, substring, keywords, actuator, arguments, cooldown_seconds, event_type, source, params, ask_first, retry_policy, debounce_seconds)

set_power_profile: Switch the machine between its power profiles - typically power-saver, balanced and performance - and report which one is active now. The profile list is read from the machine rather than assumed, because which profiles exist depends on the CPU driver: switching to one the machine does not have is refused with the valid names listed. Changes the CPU and platform power behaviour, not a per-application setting. (arguments: profile)
get_battery_status: Get the current battery charge percentage and charging state.

charger_info: Report what is powering this machine: on battery or plugged in, AC adapter or USB-C, whether USB Power Delivery is in use, and the charger's wattage when the firmware reports it, plus battery charge and rate.

power_action: Suspend (sleep), hibernate, restart or shut down this computer, or cancel a scheduled restart/shutdown. Restart and shutdown happen after one minute and can be cancelled. Requires the 'power-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action)

train.say: how do you spell necessary?
train.positives_desc: spell_word: Check how a word is spelled, offline, and suggest the closest correct spellings - 'how do you spell necessary', 'is it recieve or receive'. (arguments: word)

negatives.desc: define_word: What a word means, from Wiktionary. Requires the web sense and privacy mode off. (arguments: word)

alarm: Alarm clock: set an alarm at a time of day (once, or repeating daily/weekdays/weekends/chosen days), list alarms, say when the next one is, change one's time or label, snooze the one that just rang, or delete one. Examples: 'set an alarm for 7am', 'alarm for 6:30 on weekdays', 'when is my next alarm?', 'change my 7am alarm to 7:30', 'snooze', 'delete the 7am alarm'. Times may be words ('7am', '7:30 pm', 'tomorrow 6:45'). It rings with a notification and the alarm sound even if the assistant is closed; it is held by systemd --user, so a reboot drops it until alarms are next listed, which re-arms it. (arguments: action, time, label, repeat, id, new_time, new_label, minutes)

ask_user: Ask the user a clarifying question and wait for their answer, with 2 to 4 short options they can pick. Use this whenever a request is genuinely ambiguous - especially when several files or devices could match. Do not guess instead, and do not ask when one option is obviously right. In a headless session there is nobody to answer and this will say so. (arguments: question, options)

calendar_edit: Change the user's calendar: 'create' adds an event to the default calendar (title, start, optional duration or end, location); 'move' reschedules an event found by its current time and/or title to new_start; 'cancel' deletes one. Times in words: 'tomorrow 3pm', 'friday 5 pm', '2026-10-09 14:00'. Move and cancel ask the person to confirm. Ambiguous matches are refused with the candidates. Requires the 'calendar-write-enabled' consent key (move/cancel also 'calendar-read-enabled'). No invitations are sent. (arguments: action, title, start, duration, end, new_start, location, notes)

conversations: The user's saved Chronoa conversations. list: recent ones; search: find what was said in earlier conversations (query); open: continue one (which = title or id); new: start a fresh one; rename (which, title); copy: duplicate one to try another way, optionally keeping only its first keep_turns user messages; export: save one as Markdown (path); delete: remove one permanently (needs 'file-delete-enabled'). (arguments: action, which, query, title, path, keep_turns)
generate_password: Generate a strong random password, or a passphrase of random words, and copy it to the clipboard (it is never said or shown in the reply). (arguments: kind, length, symbols)

notes: Keep your own notes in a plain list stored on this machine: 'add' one from 'text', 'list' them, 'search' by text or id, 'remove' one by 'id'. Never sent to a model. For what the assistant itself believes and uses in its replies, use remember_fact instead. (arguments: action, text, query, id)

train.say: Look up who a domain or address is registered to.
train.positives_desc: whois_lookup: Look up who a domain or IP address is registered to: the registrar, when it was created, when it expires, its status and its name servers. Obeys privacy mode, because the answer can name a person. Tells a registry's rate-limit refusal apart from 'this domain is not registered', which are very different facts. Read-only, though it necessarily contacts a registry outside this machine. (arguments: domain)

negatives.desc: search_documents: Search inside the user's files by their contents, using the desktop's own search index (LocalSearch on GNOME, Baloo on Plasma). Requires the 'document-search-enabled' consent key. (arguments: query, kind, limit)

search_file_contents: Search inside text files under a directory for a literal string, and report which files contain it and on which lines. Skips binary files and very large files, and says how many it skipped. (arguments: text, path, file_pattern, case_sensitive, max_matches)

search_my_files: Search your own files by meaning - documents, notes, code - in a directory you choose, or your home if you name none. 'search': what matches a few words. 'reindex': read the directory and build or refresh the index (needed before the first search). 'status': what would be indexed and whether this machine can search by meaning. Needs the 'file-index-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, query, path, limit)

web_search: Look something up on the web and return what the pages actually say: facts, prices, how-tos, anything no more specific tool covers. Give a search query, a specific URL, or both. For a scholarly question - a paper, a preprint, prior work, 'what does the research say' - set source=arxiv and it searches the arXiv preprint archive instead of the web. For news headlines use news; to click, fill in or book something on a site use browse. Requires the web sense to be enabled and privacy mode to be off. (arguments: query, url, source)
my_ip_address: This computer's IP addresses: local (LAN) addresses per network interface, and the public internet address when the web sense is on.

device_i2c: Read a register on an I2C device, or write one with the 'i2c-write-enabled' consent key. Reading needs no permission; writing is listed as destructive because a write to the wrong register can erase an EEPROM's calibration, and register ranges that do that are refused outright. (arguments: bus, address, register, action, value)

dns_lookup: Look a hostname or address up in DNS and report what came back: the addresses, or the mail servers, name servers, TXT records, certificate records or other records a name publishes, and whether the answer is DNSSEC-signed and valid. Distinguishes 'this name does not exist' from 'the resolver did not answer', because those have different fixes. Obeys privacy mode, since the query goes to a resolver outside this machine. Read-only. (arguments: name, type)

train.say: Permanently empty the desktop trash.
train.positives_desc: empty_trash: Permanently delete everything in the desktop trash, after listing what is in there first. There is no way to undo this, so it requires the 'trash-empty-enabled' consent key. Use 'list' to see the contents without emptying anything. (arguments: action)

negatives.desc: delete_file: Delete a file or folder by moving it to the desktop trash, where it stays recoverable. This is how you clear something out. The whole folder goes as one item and can be restored from the trash - nothing in this project is deleted permanently, so there is no faster or 'real' delete to reach for instead. Requires the 'file-delete-enabled' consent key. (arguments: path)

empty_directories: Find directories under a path that hold nothing at all. Use for 'clean up empty folders', 'what are these leftover directories', 'tidy this up'. Empty means rmdir would succeed - a directory holding only sub-directories is not empty - and one that cannot be read is not empty either. Reports what it found and removes nothing. Read-only. (arguments: path, limit)

desktop_setting: Read or change one desktop setting from a fixed list: animations (window and menu animations); cursor_size (mouse pointer size in pixels (24 is normal; 32, 48, 64 are larger)); single_click (open files and folders with a single click); clock_24h (show the top-bar clock in 24-hour format); clock_seconds (show seconds in the top-bar clock); battery_percentage (show the battery percentage in the top bar); hot_corner (open the overview when the pointer hits the top-left corner); natural_scroll (touchpad natural (reverse) scrolling); tap_to_click (tap the touchpad to click). Changing requires the 'appearance-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: setting, value)
cleanup_report: Report what could be cleaned up to free disk space - trash, caches, the system log, unused Flatpak runtimes - with sizes. Reads only; deletes nothing.

conversations: The user's saved Chronoa conversations. list: recent ones; search: find what was said in earlier conversations (query); open: continue one (which = title or id); new: start a fresh one; rename (which, title); copy: duplicate one to try another way, optionally keeping only its first keep_turns user messages; export: save one as Markdown (path); delete: remove one permanently (needs 'file-delete-enabled'). (arguments: action, which, query, title, path, keep_turns)

set_sleep_inhibit: Report what is currently holding the machine awake, or take a bounded hold so it does not sleep for a while, or release ours. Use for 'keep it awake while I...' - a long install, a backup, a test run. Scoped and self-lapsing; to change the machine's idle timeout permanently use set_screensaver instead. Gated by 'sleep-inhibit-enabled' consent key; reporting needs no such permission. (arguments: action, reason, seconds)

cleanup_apply: Actually free the disk space cleanup_report measured: empty your cache folder, or remove Flatpak runtimes no app uses. Both are recoverable or provably unused. Requires the 'cleanup-enabled' consent key. The system log is not here - that needs root, which Chronoa cannot ask for from inside a tool call. (arguments: target)

train.say: Remind me to call mom tomorrow at 6pm
train.positives_desc: reminders: A dated list of reminders you can keep coming back to: add one, list what is still due, mark one done, or remove one. Optionally with a due time in words, e.g. 'tomorrow 9am' or 'in 3 hours'. (arguments: action, number, text, due)

negatives.desc: watch: Your MoYoung/Da Fit smartwatch: 'summary' (steps, distance, calories for 3 days, last night's sleep stages, today's stress, workouts), 'measure' a heart rate, blood oxygen or blood pressure on the wrist (takes up to a minute), read 'settings', 'set' one (step_goal, time_format 12h/24h, units metric/imperial, raise_to_wake, sedentary_reminder, other_app_notifications, power_saving, heart_rate_auto_interval, do_not_disturb '22:00-07:00'), 'sync_time', 'notify' (show a message on the watch), or set the 'profile' (height, weight, age, gender - weight is never measured by the watch). Requires the 'bluetooth-gatt-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, device, what, setting, value, sender, text, kind, height_cm, weight_kg, age, gender)

bluetooth_call: Use a paired Android phone as a Bluetooth speakerphone, with no cable and no app on the phone. 'status' says whether a phone is connected as a hands-free unit, whether a call is in progress, and which audio profile its call audio arrived on. 'dial' places a call - 'dial number="+441234567890"' - asking you to confirm first, because it rings someone. 'answer' and 'hangup' work on a call already in progress. 'audio' reports where the call's voice is going and names anything missing from that path, and 'profile' switches the card between wide-band hfp_hf and narrow-band hsp_hs. The phone stays the radio; this routes the voice to this computer's speakers and microphone. Needs the phone connected over Bluetooth, not merely paired, and the 'bluetooth-call-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, card, profile, to, number)

calendar_edit: Change the user's calendar: 'create' adds an event to the default calendar (title, start, optional duration or end, location); 'move' reschedules an event found by its current time and/or title to new_start; 'cancel' deletes one. Requires the 'calendar-write-enabled' consent key (move/cancel also 'calendar-read-enabled'). No invitations are sent. (arguments: action, title, start, duration, end, new_start, location, notes)

calendar_events: List events on the user's calendars (GNOME calendars and online accounts): today, tomorrow, this week, or the next few hours. Requires the 'calendar-read-enabled' consent key. (arguments: range, hours)

phone: The user's paired phone via GSConnect/KDE Connect: status (reachable, battery), ring it to find it, ping it, share a file or link to it; read text messages ('messages': latest, from a contact, or unread only); send a text message ('send': to a contact name or number, or omit contact to reply to the latest conversation) with exactly the text given - draft it first; or 'call' a contact or number (opens the phone's dialer). The user confirms every message and call before it goes. Requires the 'phone-control-enabled' consent key; reading needs 'phone-messages-read-enabled', sending and calling 'phone-messages-send-enabled'. (arguments: action, device, target, contact, text, unread_only, limit)

date_math: Date arithmetic: days until a date ('how many days until 25 December'), the date N days/weeks/months from a date ('what date is 45 days from now'), days between two dates, or the weekday of a date. (arguments: operation, date, other_date, amount, unit)

train.say: show my bluetooth devices
train.positives_desc: bluetooth_devices: List paired Bluetooth devices (and which are connected), or connect / disconnect one by its name, e.g. 'connect my headphones'. (arguments: action, name)

negatives.desc: toggle_bluetooth: Turn the Bluetooth adapter on or off, or report its state and the paired devices. Requires the 'bluetooth-control-enabled' consent key; reporting needs no such permission. (arguments: action)

bluetooth_call: Use a paired Android phone as a Bluetooth speakerphone, with no cable and no app on the phone. 'status' says whether a phone is connected as a hands-free unit, whether a call is in progress, and which audio profile its call audio arrived on. 'dial' places a call - 'dial number="+441234567890"' - asking you to confirm first, because it rings someone. 'answer' and 'hangup' work on a call already in progress. 'audio' reports where the call's voice is going and names anything missing from that path, and 'profile' switches the card between wide-band hfp_hf and narrow-band hsp_hs. The phone stays the radio; this routes the voice to this computer's speakers and microphone. Needs the phone connected over Bluetooth, not merely paired, and the 'bluetooth-call-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, card, profile, to, number)

bluetooth_gatt: Read what a paired Bluetooth Low Energy device says about itself - a watch's or headset's battery, a heart-rate strap's live reading, which services a band offers. 'list': every paired device and whether it speaks this protocol. 'services': what one exposes. 'read': one stored value. 'listen': a live reading of something the device only pushes, e.g. heart rate - 'nothing arrived' is the truthful answer when the device is not measuring. Speakers, headphones and car stereios are older Bluetooth and expose nothing here, which is a true answer, not a failure; wearables, bands, straps, smart tags and thermometers answer. Needs 'bluetooth-gatt-enabled' and the device must be connected. (arguments: action, device, seconds, characteristic)

usb_devices: What is plugged into this machine's USB ports (mice, phones, webcams, sticks, with their speed), and every Thunderbolt/USB4 device with whether it is authorised to work. Use for 'what's plugged in', 'why doesn't my dock work', 'is my webcam connected'. The USB list uses the 'usb-sense-enabled' switch. Read-only.

find_device: Make a paired Bluetooth watch, band or tag buzz or ring so the person can find it - 'where is my watch', 'find my band'. Works on devices with the standard Immediate Alert service and on MoYoung (Da Fit) watches; anything else is refused rather than sent an unknown command. The device must be in range. Requires the 'bluetooth-gatt-enabled' consent key. (arguments: device)

set_hostname: Report this computer's name (hostname), or rename it - the name other devices on the network and in Bluetooth see. The name must be letters, digits and hyphens only. Renaming requires the 'hostname-control-enabled' consent key and the administrator password; reporting needs neither. (arguments: action, name)

android_device: An Android phone connected with USB debugging (adb). devices: which are connected; info: model, Android version, battery, storage; screenshot: save the phone's screen as a PNG; apps: installed apps (query filters); push: copy a file to the phone (to, default /sdcard/Download); pull: copy a file from the phone; open_url: open a web link on the phone. Requires 'phone-control-enabled'. (arguments: action, serial, path, to, url, query, output)

train.say: Month calendar.
train.positives_desc: calendar_month: Show the calendar for a month (default this month), with today marked. (arguments: month, year)

Times in words: 'tomorrow 3pm', 'friday 5 pm', '2026-10-09 14:00'. Move and cancel ask the person to confirm. Ambiguous matches are refused with the candidates. Requires the 'calendar-write-enabled' consent key (move/cancel also 'calendar-read-enabled'). No invitations are sent. (arguments: action, title, start, duration, end, new_start, location, notes)

calendar_events: List events on the user's calendars (GNOME calendars and online accounts): today, tomorrow, this week, or the next few hours. Requires the 'calendar-read-enabled' consent key. (arguments: range, hours)

date_math: Date arithmetic: days until a date ('how many days until 25 December'), the date N days/weeks/months from a date ('what date is 45 days from now'), days between two dates, or the weekday of a date. (arguments: operation, date, other_date, amount, unit)
data_usage: How much internet data this computer has used today and this month, per network interface (from vnStat).

set_locale: Report the system language and regional formats, list the locales available on this machine, or change one: the system language, or the date format (British day/month or American month/day order), number format (decimal comma or point), money, measurement or paper size (e.g. what='dates', locale='en_GB.UTF-8'). Takes effect at the next login. Changing requires the 'locale-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, locale, what)

manage_triggers: Arm, list, or remove automatic rules that run a Chronoa action when a perception matches - for example, notify when the battery sense reports low. A rule names one already-whitelisted skill; it cannot run an arbitrary command or an LLM-authored prompt. Listing needs no permission; arming or disarming requires the 'trigger-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, name, sense, match_mode, substring, keywords, actuator, arguments, cooldown_seconds, event_type, source, params, ask_first, retry_policy, debounce_seconds)

routines: Save a routine: a short phrase (e.g. 'good morning', 'leaving work') that later runs a whole request, e.g. 'tell me the weather, my calendar today and the top news'. Also list or delete routines. Saving runs nothing; saying the phrase later runs the request. (arguments: action, name, request, phrases)

train.say: what's my IP address
train.positives_desc: my_ip_address: This computer's IP addresses: local (LAN) addresses per network interface, and the public internet address when the web sense is on.

negatives.desc: check_port: Check whether a specific port on a specific host accepts connections from this machine, and say why it does not - refused (the host is up, nothing is listening), timed out (a firewall, or a host that is off), or the name does not resolve. Use for 'is my server reachable', 'why can nothing connect to it', 'is port 443 open on that box'. Opens exactly one connection and sends nothing; it is not a scan. (arguments: host, port)

ping_host: Ping a named host or IP address and report whether it answers, how long the replies take and how many were lost. Use this when a specific host is slow or unreachable; 'check_internet' only answers whether the internet works at all. (arguments: host, count)

trace_route: Trace the network path to a host: every router along the way, how much of the traffic each one dropped, and how many milliseconds it took. Use when something specific is slow or unreachable, which is different from whether the internet works at all. (arguments: host, probes)

whois_lookup: Look up who a domain or IP address is registered to: the registrar, when it was created, when it expires, its status and its name servers. Obeys privacy mode, because the answer can name a person. Tells a registry's rate-limit refusal apart from 'this domain is not registered', which are very different facts. Read-only, though it necessarily contacts a registry outside this machine. (arguments: domain)

bandwidth_to_host: Measure how fast this machine can send data to another machine over the network, using a controlled iperf3 transfer. Use for 'why is my NAS slow', 'how fast is my network to the server', 'is the bottleneck the network or the disk'. Needs iperf3 running on the other machine - ask for loopback to measure this machine against itself. Read-only: it transfers data and writes nothing. (arguments: host, port, seconds)
tailscale_status: Tailscale status: whether it is connected, this machine's Tailscale IP, and which of your other devices are online.

discover_hosts: Find which devices are on this network right now, by asking rather than by reading the cache - so devices that have never talked to this machine are found too. Reports an address and a hardware address for each, and counts devices answering on more than one address. The range is always the private network this machine is on; pass network= for a different private range, and a public one is refused. Connects to nothing it finds and reads no packet contents. Needs raw-socket access, so unprivileged it may report that rather than a partial sweep. (arguments: interface, network)

train.say: what's 15% of 2400
train.positives_desc: calculate: Evaluate arithmetic and percentages ('15% of 2400'), or convert between units. Handles the four operations, powers, parentheses, factorial, permutations and combinations (perm/nPr, comb/nCr), gcd, lcm, sqrt, exp, log, ln, trig and inverse trig, and pi/e/tau - exact for whole numbers. For algebra with variables, derivatives, integrals, limits or equations, use solve_math. Converts length, mass, volume, time, data, pressure, frequency, power, energy and temperature, in the units a person actually meets - say '200 km to miles' or '70kg in lb'. Runs entirely on this machine with no network call. Refuses to guess: a percentage needs a number to apply to, and converting between quantities that measure different things is an error rather than a number. (arguments: expression)

negatives.desc: edit_image: Edit a picture (for faces or backgrounds use photo_video) and save the result as a new file next to it: resize (width and/or height, or percent), compress (quality, or to under a size in KB), crop, upscale (2-4x), rotate, flip, grayscale, a look (sepia, vignette, sketch, paint, enhance), strip metadata (location/camera), or convert format. Several edits can be combined in one call. For effects that depend on what is in the picture (blur faces, blur the background) use photo_video. (arguments: path, width, height, percent, upscale, quality, max_kb, crop, rotate, flip, grayscale, look, strip_metadata, format)
encode_text: Encode or decode text: base64, url (percent-encoding), hex, binary, rot13, morse. (arguments: text, scheme, direction)

process_cost: What each running program is COSTING this machine right now, measured over the last second rather than as a snapshot: percent CPU split into user and system time, how much memory it holds, page faults (including the major ones that mean it is thrashing), and how many kB a second it is reading and writing. Answers 'what is using my CPU', 'what is making my computer slow', 'what is writing to my disk all the time', 'which program is swapping', 'why did everything freeze'. Use this when the machine feels slow; use list_processes to see what is running and disk_activity to see whether the disk itself is busy. Read-only; nothing is started, stopped or changed.

thread_activity: Show the individual THREADS of a process - or of the whole machine - with the CPU each is using right now and the kernel function it is blocked in. Use for 'which thread is using the CPU', 'this program is at 300 percent', 'what is this thread waiting on', 'why is this stuck', 'which of these threads is busy'. Goes one level below process_detail and list_processes, which report one figure for the whole process and cannot tell a program with one hot thread from one using every core evenly. Read-only; nothing is sampled with a tool, attached to or changed. (arguments: pid)

train.say: lock my screen
train.positives_desc: lock_screen: Lock this session so a password is needed to come back to it. Uses the session's own mechanism so the same thing happens as the desktop's Lock button. Requires the 'screen-lock-enabled' consent key.

negatives.desc: file_locks: Show who holds a file lock, and on what - the answer to "why won't this file save" and "why did my write fail with EAGAIN". A WRITE lock blocks another writer; a READ lock is shared and usually harmless. Use for 'who has this file locked', 'what is holding a lock', 'why can't I write this file', 'is this file locked'. Give a path to check one file; omit it for every lock on the machine. Reads the kernel's own lock table (/proc/locks), so it needs no binary and no privilege. Read-only; nothing is polled, changed or broken. (arguments: path)

screen_to_phone: Show this computer's screen on a paired phone, over the Bluetooth network. 'status': could this be shared here at all, and what is missing if not. 'start': ask the desktop to share the screen and serve it to the phone - the desktop shows its own 'Share screen' dialog, which only the person can answer. 'stop': end it and close the portal session. The picture goes over Bluetooth, so it is not on Wi-Fi, but it is the whole screen - which is why this needs the 'screen-share-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action)

set_screensaver: Report or change how long the machine waits before the screen blanks, and whether it then demands a password. The two are reported separately, because blanking without locking leaves anyone who walks up to the machine able to use it. Requires the 'idle-timeout-enabled' consent key; reporting needs no such permission. (arguments: action, blank_after_minutes, lock)

accessibility: Turn an accessibility feature on or off, or report them all: screen reader, on-screen keyboard, magnifier (zoom), large text, high contrast, reduce motion (animations), sticky keys. (arguments: feature, enabled)

set_privacy: Control the machine's privacy: mute or unmute the microphone, enable or disable a camera, or blank the screen. Muting the microphone is a user-level stream mute that any new application can override, and the reply says so rather than implying the hardware is off. Disabling a camera needs root and is only possible on drivers that expose a disable control, so a device with no such control is reported as unsupported rather than disabled. Blanking works on X11; under Wayland it would need a permission prompt, so the idle timeout is offered instead. Every action says how to undo it. (arguments: action, device)

manage_triggers: Arm, list, or remove automatic rules that run a Chronoa action when a perception matches - for example, notify when the battery sense reports low. A rule names one already-whitelisted skill; it cannot run an arbitrary command or an LLM-authored prompt. Listing needs no permission; arming or disarming requires the 'trigger-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, name, sense, match_mode, substring, keywords, actuator, arguments, cooldown_seconds, event_type, source, params, ask_first, retry_policy, debounce_seconds)

temp_files: Find junk, temporary and leftover files by NAME - editor swap and lock files (*.tmp, *.swp, *~, .#*, ~$*, .goutputstream-*), OS metadata (.DS_Store, Thumbs.db, desktop.ini), unfinished downloads (*.crdownload, *.part, *.filepart), merge leftovers (*.orig, *.rej) and core dumps. Use for 'what junk is in here', 'what can I clean up', 'what temporary files do I have'. A name is a guess and the answer says so: nothing is deleted, moved or changed, and a file this cannot read is reported rather than counted as clean. Core dumps are confirmed by reading the ELF header, because a name like `core` is usually a source directory or a JavaScript module. Read-only. (arguments: path, limit)

train.say: what did we talk about the router last week?
train.positives_desc: conversations: The user's saved Chronoa conversations. list: recent ones; search: find what was said in earlier conversations (query); open: continue one (which = title or id); new: start a fresh one; rename (which, title); copy: duplicate one to try another way, optionally keeping only its first keep_turns user messages; export: save one as Markdown (path); delete: remove one permanently (needs 'file-delete-enabled'). (arguments: action, which, query, title, path, keep_turns)

negatives.desc: search_my_files: Search your own files by meaning - documents, notes, code - in a directory you choose, or your home if you name none. 'search': what matches a few words. 'reindex': read the directory and build or refresh the index (needed before the first search). 'status': what would be indexed and whether this machine can search by meaning. Needs the 'file-index-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, query, path, limit)

undo_last_change: Put a file back the way Chronoa last found it, by restoring the content recorded just before Chronoa's own last edit to it. Undoes Chronoa's recent writes only - NOT git history, NOT changes you made in an editor or a shell, and only while a recorded pre-image is still held. Requires the 'file-edit-enabled' consent key. (arguments: path, list, steps)

search_documents: Search inside the user's files by their contents, using the desktop's own search index (LocalSearch on GNOME, Baloo on Plasma). Requires the 'document-search-enabled' consent key. (arguments: query, kind, limit)

search_file_contents: Search inside text files under a directory for a literal string, and report which files contain it and on which lines. Skips binary files and very large files, and says how many it skipped. (arguments: text, path, file_pattern, case_sensitive, max_matches)

web_search: Look something up on the web and return what the pages actually say: facts, prices, how-tos, anything no more specific tool covers. Give a search query, a specific URL, or both. For a scholarly question - a paper, a preprint, prior work, 'what does the research say' - set source=arxiv and it searches the arXiv preprint archive instead of the web. For news headlines use news; to click, fill in or book something on a site use browse. Requires the web sense to be enabled and privacy mode to be off. (arguments: query, url, source)

calendar_events: List events on the user's calendars (GNOME calendars and online accounts): today, tomorrow, this week, or the next few hours. Requires the 'calendar-read-enabled' consent key. (arguments: range, hours)

date_math: Date arithmetic: days until a date ('how many days until 25 December'), the date N days/weeks/months from a date ('what date is 45 days from now'), days between two dates, or the weekday of a date. (arguments: operation, date, other_date, amount, unit)

train.say: What changed today.
train.positives_desc: find_recently_modified: List files under a directory whose recorded modification time is within the last N days, newest first. Use this to answer 'what did I change today'. This is a timestamp, so a tool that preserves or sets times (tar, rsync, cp -p) can move an entry without the content changing. (arguments: path, within_days, pattern, limit)

negatives.desc: get_datetime: The current date and time here. For the time in another city or country, use get_world_time.

calendar_events: List events on the user's calendars (GNOME calendars and online accounts): today, tomorrow, this week, or the next few hours. Requires the 'calendar-read-enabled' consent key. (arguments: range, hours)

git_inspect: Report a git working tree: what has changed and is not committed, the diff of those changes, recent commits, or the current branch and how far it is from its upstream; also the stashed work and the reflog (the record that survives rebases and amends). Reports UNKNOWN - never 'clean tree' - when git is missing, the folder is not a repository, or git fails. Requires the 'git-sense-enabled' consent key. (arguments: path, subcommand, revision, since, context_lines)
get_world_time: The current time and date in ANOTHER city, country or time zone, e.g. 'what time is it in Tokyo'. For the time here, use get_datetime. (arguments: place)
calendar_month: Show the calendar for a month (default this month), with today marked. (arguments: month, year)

convert_currency: Convert an amount of money between currencies (rupees, dollars, euros, pounds, yen, ...) at today's ECB reference rate. Requires the web sense and privacy mode off. (arguments: amount, from_currency, to_currency)
data_usage: How much internet data this computer has used today and this month, per network interface (from vnStat).

train.say: Start a 2 gigabyte virtual machine and boot it with UEFI firmware.
train.positives_desc: vm: Run a virtual machine with QEMU and drive it like a browser: launch it with a visible window on the desktop and a QMP control socket beside it, photograph its screen, send key combinations, type text into it, move and click its pointer (percentages of its screen), check its power state, and stop it. Requires the 'vm-control-enabled' consent key, off by default. Listing the VMs already running is `list_vms` (virsh) or this skill's list action; this one starts and drives them. (arguments: action, name, memory_mb, iso, disk, display, firmware, tpm, keys, text, x, y, button)

negatives.desc: boot_report: How the last boot went: total boot time split into firmware, loader, kernel and userspace, the services that took longest to start, when the machine booted and whether it shut down cleanly before, and which EFI entry the firmware will boot by default. Use for 'why does it boot slowly', 'did it crash last time'. Boot history uses the 'boots-sense-enabled' switch. Read-only. (arguments: top)

open_application: Open or launch an installed application by name or by kind, e.g. 'firefox', 'files', 'settings', 'music player', 'text editor'. Not for websites: use browse to open a site and work on it. (arguments: name)

firmware_updates: List firmware updates fwupd knows for this machine's devices (BIOS, SSD, dock, touchpad...) and what each fixes, plus the firmware versions this machine is running. Read-only; nothing is installed.

open_file: Open one specific file or folder (by its path) using the desktop's default application for it - the same thing double-clicking it would do. To launch an app such as the file manager, use open_application. (arguments: path)

open_settings: Open the system Settings app at a specific page, e.g. 'wifi', 'bluetooth', 'display', 'sound', 'power', 'privacy', 'keyboard', 'mouse', 'touchpad', 'printers', 'users', 'about', 'date_time', 'region', 'notifications', 'background', 'accessibility'. GNOME and KDE Plasma. Use open_application for Settings without a page. (arguments: page)

oom_score: Which process the kernel would kill if memory ran out, and whether it has killed anything already. Reports how much time this machine has spent stalled waiting on memory, the kernel's own ranking of who would go first, any process somebody deliberately marked as more expendable, and how many processes the kernel has OOM-killed since boot. Answers 'who would the kernel kill', 'why did my program disappear', 'is my machine short on memory', 'has anything been killed', 'what would happen if I opened more'. Use this when something vanished or the machine stalled; use list_processes to see what is running and the memory sense to see how much is used. Read-only; nothing is adjusted and nothing is killed.

open_files: Find which programs have a file, directory or network socket open. Use for 'what is using this file', 'why can't I delete this', 'what has my disk open', 'which process is holding that socket'. Names the holding program with its full command line, and flags deleted files whose space cannot be reclaimed. Reads only this user's processes unless run as root. Read-only: it lists open handles and never closes one. (arguments: path, pid, limit)

train.say: Outline a code project: files, classes and functions.
train.positives_desc: project_outline: Outline a code project or one source file: files, classes and functions with line numbers, the most referenced first, so a large project fits. query focuses on names or paths containing it. Python is parsed exactly; other languages by definition patterns. (arguments: path, query, max_lines)

negatives.desc: qr_code: read: decode every QR code and barcode in a picture (path) or on the screen (screen=true, needs the vision consent). create: make a QR code PNG of text (a URL, Wi-Fi details, a note) at output. (arguments: action, path, screen, text, output)

search_my_files: Search your own files by meaning - documents, notes, code - in a directory you choose, or your home if you name none. 'search': what matches a few words. 'reindex': read the directory and build or refresh the index (needed before the first search). 'status': what would be indexed and whether this machine can search by meaning. Needs the 'file-index-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, query, path, limit)

cloud_files: See what is in this machine's configured cloud storage remotes - which remotes rclone knows, how many objects and bytes each holds, and what is at the top level of one. Use for 'what is in my cloud drive', 'is anything in the bucket', 'how big is my remote'. Read-only: it never copies, syncs or deletes anything. A machine with no remotes says so, because that means there is nowhere off-machine for anything to go. (arguments: remote, path)

compare_files: Show what is different between two text files, as a unified diff. Reports 'identical' when they match. Use this to compare two versions of a config, or to see what a change actually did. (arguments: path_a, path_b, context_lines)

duplicate_files: Find files with identical content under a directory, and how much space the copies waste. Use for 'why is my disk full', 'are there duplicates in my Downloads', 'where is my space going'. Reports verified groups only - same size is evidence, a matching hash is proof - and never marks one copy as the original. Read-only: it hashes and lists, and deletes nothing. (arguments: path, limit)

files_by_name: Find every file with a given name under a directory, with sizes and modification dates, so you can see whether they are copies. Use for 'where are all my report.docx', 'how many copies of this do I have', 'which is the newest'. Reports the newest and whether the sizes agree, and does NOT claim the contents match - duplicate_files answers that. Deletes nothing. (arguments: name, path, case_sensitive)

find_files: Find files and folders by name under a directory, using a wildcard pattern such as '*.log' or 'report*'. Matches on the name only and never opens the files. To see what is in one folder, use list_directory. (arguments: pattern, path, include_hidden, max_results)

train.say: are there any system updates?
train.positives_desc: check_updates: Check whether this machine has package updates waiting, without installing anything and without needing root. Works on Arch and other pacman systems.

negatives.desc: firmware_updates: List firmware updates fwupd knows for this machine's devices (BIOS, SSD, dock, touchpad...) and what each fixes, plus the firmware versions this machine is running. Read-only; nothing is installed.

system_history: What this machine's CPU, disk, memory or paging was doing earlier, from the sysstat accounting records rather than a live reading. Use for 'was this busy last night', 'what was using the disk at lunchtime', 'why was the fan loud earlier'. Says plainly when no history has been recorded, because that is not the same as the machine having been idle. Read-only. (arguments: topic)

system_info: Describe the machine Chronoa is running on: distribution, kernel, architecture, uptime, load, memory, CPU count, whether this is a desktop session or a container, and the hardware identity (make, model, board, BIOS version).

cleanup_apply: Actually free the disk space cleanup_report measured: empty your cache folder, or remove Flatpak runtimes no app uses. Both are recoverable or provably unused. Requires the 'cleanup-enabled' consent key. The system log is not here - that needs root, which Chronoa cannot ask for from inside a tool call. (arguments: target)
cleanup_report: Report what could be cleaned up to free disk space - trash, caches, the system log, unused Flatpak runtimes - with sizes. Reads only; deletes nothing.
get_clipboard: Read the current contents of the system clipboard.
set_clipboard: Write text to the system clipboard. (arguments: text)

train.say: Report or change the system timezone.
train.positives_desc: set_timezone: Report the current system timezone, list the ones available, or change it. Changing it needs root and requires the 'timezone-control-enabled' consent key; reporting needs no such permission. Validates the zone against the system's own list first. (arguments: action, timezone)

negatives.desc: system_history: What this machine's CPU, disk, memory or paging was doing earlier, from the sysstat accounting records rather than a live reading. Use for 'was this busy last night', 'what was using the disk at lunchtime', 'why was the fan loud earlier'. Says plainly when no history has been recorded, because that is not the same as the machine having been idle. Read-only. (arguments: topic)

system_info: Describe the machine Chronoa is running on: distribution, kernel, architecture, uptime, load, memory, CPU count, whether this is a desktop session or a container, and the hardware identity (make, model, board, BIOS version).

undo_last_change: Put a file back the way Chronoa last found it, by restoring the content recorded just before Chronoa's own last edit to it. Undoes Chronoa's recent writes only - NOT git history, NOT changes you made in an editor or a shell, and only while a recorded pre-image is still held. Requires the 'file-edit-enabled' consent key. (arguments: path, list, steps)
cleanup_report: Report what could be cleaned up to free disk space - trash, caches, the system log, unused Flatpak runtimes - with sizes. Reads only; deletes nothing.

set_locale: Report the system language and regional formats, list the locales available on this machine, or change one: the system language, or the date format (British day/month or American month/day order), number format (decimal comma or point), money, measurement or paper size (e.g. what='dates', locale='en_GB.UTF-8'). Takes effect at the next login. Changing requires the 'locale-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, locale, what)

alarm: Alarm clock: set an alarm at a time of day (once, or repeating daily/weekdays/weekends/chosen days), list alarms, say when the next one is, change one's time or label, snooze the one that just rang, or delete one. Examples: 'set an alarm for 7am', 'alarm for 6:30 on weekdays', 'when is my next alarm?', 'change my 7am alarm to 7:30', 'snooze', 'delete the 7am alarm'. Times may be words ('7am', '7:30 pm', 'tomorrow 6:45'). It rings with a notification and the alarm sound even if the assistant is closed; it is held by systemd --user, so a reboot drops it until alarms are next listed, which re-arms it. (arguments: action, time, label, repeat, id, new_time, new_label, minutes)

calendar_edit: Change the user's calendar: 'create' adds an event to the default calendar (title, start, optional duration or end, location); 'move' reschedules an event found by its current time and/or title to new_start; 'cancel' deletes one. Times in words: 'tomorrow 3pm', 'friday 5 pm', '2026-10-09 14:00'. Move and cancel ask the person to confirm. Ambiguous matches are refused with the candidates. Requires the 'calendar-write-enabled' consent key (move/cancel also 'calendar-read-enabled'). No invitations are sent. (arguments: action, title, start, duration, end, new_start, location, notes)

train.say: how loud is it right now?
train.positives_desc: get_volume: Get the current volume and mute state of an audio output, or the default one. On a machine with more than one output - several monitors, headphones and a dock - 'the volume' is ambiguous, so pass the device exactly as `wpctl status` prints it to ask about a specific one. (arguments: device)

negatives.desc: set_volume: Set the system output volume to an exact percentage. (arguments: percent, device)

cpu_frequency: What the processor is doing right now: which speed governor it is in, roughly what speed it is running at, and the range its hardware allows. Use after setting a power mode, to see whether the machine actually took it up - 'why is my fan so loud', 'is my CPU being throttled', 'did performance mode do anything'. Read-only; changes nothing.
click_pointer: Click a mouse button at the current pointer position. Requires the 'input-control-enabled' consent key (separate from the vision sense) to be enabled. (arguments: button, count)
read_audio: Read an audio file's basics out loud: how long it is, its codec, sample rate, channels, and bitrate. The original is never modified. (arguments: path)

read_image: Read a picture's basics out loud: width by height, format, and colour type, plus file size. For what the picture says, use read_document on it. The original is never modified. (arguments: path)

read_video: Read a video's basics out loud (for subtitles or what was said use recording): how long it is, its resolution, its video codec, whether it has audio, and its bitrate. Add keyframes=true to also save the moments the image changes. The original is never modified. (arguments: path, keyframes)

system_history: What this machine's CPU, disk, memory or paging was doing earlier, from the sysstat accounting records rather than a live reading. Use for 'was this busy last night', 'what was using the disk at lunchtime', 'why was the fan loud earlier'. Says plainly when no history has been recorded, because that is not the same as the machine having been idle. Read-only. (arguments: topic)

train.say: Minimize, maximize, move or resize a window.
train.positives_desc: arrange_window: Minimize, maximize, unmaximize, make fullscreen, leave fullscreen, move, resize, or send a window to another workspace, by window id from list_windows or by part of its title. move takes x and y, resize takes width and height (pixels), set_workspace takes a 0-based workspace. Nothing is closed; close_window does that. (arguments: action, window_id, title_contains, x, y, width, height, workspace)

negatives.desc: close_window: Ask a window to close, the way its close button would - the application still gets the chance to ask about unsaved work. Requires the 'window-close-enabled' consent key. Works on X11, Plasma and GNOME (GTK4 apps, or any app with Chronoa's window control extension). (arguments: window_id, title_contains)
move_pointer: Move the pointer to absolute screen coordinates. Requires the 'input-control-enabled' consent key (separate from the vision sense) to be enabled. (arguments: x, y)

vm: Run a virtual machine with QEMU and drive it like a browser: launch it with a visible window on the desktop and a QMP control socket beside it, photograph its screen, send key combinations, type text into it, move and click its pointer (percentages of its screen), check its power state, and stop it. Requires the 'vm-control-enabled' consent key, off by default. Listing the VMs already running is `list_vms` (virsh) or this skill's list action; this one starts and drives them. (arguments: action, name, memory_mb, iso, disk, display, firmware, tpm, keys, text, x, y, button)

focus_window: Bring a window to the front and give it keyboard focus, by window id from list_windows or by matching part of its title. Works on X11 and Plasma; on GNOME it needs Chronoa's window control extension and says so. (arguments: window_id, title_contains)

move_or_copy_file: Move or copy a file or directory to a new path. Moving a directory into itself is refused, and an existing destination is not overwritten unless asked. (arguments: source, destination, mode, overwrite)

media_control: Control music and video players: play, pause, toggle, next track, previous track, stop, restart (current track from the beginning), seek (skip ahead or go back by 'seconds'; negative goes back), or 'status' to say what is playing. (arguments: action, seconds)

browse: Open a website and do things on it for the person: find information, fill in forms, click through. Drive a web browser: navigate, read the page's text (get_text), click, type, select options, scroll, move through history, take screenshots and wait for conditions. While Chronoa's window is open this is the in-app browser the user can watch: there it opens only http(s) pages the egress policy allows, and key, hover, drag, upload_file, tabs and evaluate are not available. Otherwise it is a headless Chromium with all actions. Requires the web sense to be enabled and privacy mode to be off. (arguments: action, url, selector, text, key, value, label, files, x, y, to_x, to_y, to_selector, delta_x, delta_y, steps, repeat, tab_id, path, wait_for, timeout, settle)

train.say: Which program is using a port.
train.positives_desc: port_owner: Find which program is using a network port, or list what this machine is listening on and connected to. Read-only. (arguments: port, process, kind, listening, limit)

negatives.desc: check_port: Check whether a specific port on a specific host accepts connections from this machine, and say why it does not - refused (the host is up, nothing is listening), timed out (a firewall, or a host that is off), or the name does not resolve. Use for 'is my server reachable', 'why can nothing connect to it', 'is port 443 open on that box'. Opens exactly one connection and sends nothing; it is not a scan. (arguments: host, port)

bandwidth_to_host: Measure how fast this machine can send data to another machine over the network, using a controlled iperf3 transfer. Use for 'why is my NAS slow', 'how fast is my network to the server', 'is the bottleneck the network or the disk'. Needs iperf3 running on the other machine - ask for loopback to measure this machine against itself. Read-only: it transfers data and writes nothing. (arguments: host, port, seconds)

network_activity: Report what this machine's network is doing right now, per program: which processes are sending and receiving, and how fast each interface is moving. Use for 'what is using my bandwidth', 'why is the network slow', 'what is uploading', 'is something downloading right now'. Interface rates come from /proc/net/dev and always work; per-program rates need nethogs and can only name programs this user owns. Says which half it could not measure and why, and reports an unattributed socket as unattributed rather than guessing at a program. Read-only; nothing is changed or blocked.

open_files: Find which programs have a file, directory or network socket open. Use for 'what is using this file', 'why can't I delete this', 'what has my disk open', 'which process is holding that socket'. Names the holding program with its full command line, and flags deleted files whose space cannot be reclaimed. Reads only this user's processes unless run as root. Read-only: it lists open handles and never closes one. (arguments: path, pid, limit)

process_cost: What each running program is COSTING this machine right now, measured over the last second rather than as a snapshot: percent CPU split into user and system time, how much memory it holds, page faults (including the major ones that mean it is thrashing), and how many kB a second it is reading and writing. Answers 'what is using my CPU', 'what is making my computer slow', 'what is writing to my disk all the time', 'which program is swapping', 'why did everything freeze'. Use this when the machine feels slow; use list_processes to see what is running and disk_activity to see whether the disk itself is busy. Read-only; nothing is started, stopped or changed.

thread_activity: Show the individual THREADS of a process - or of the whole machine - with the CPU each is using right now and the kernel function it is blocked in. Use for 'which thread is using the CPU', 'this program is at 300 percent', 'what is this thread waiting on', 'why is this stuck', 'which of these threads is busy'. Goes one level below process_detail and list_processes, which report one figure for the whole process and cannot tell a program with one hot thread from one using every core evenly. Read-only; nothing is sampled with a tool, attached to or changed. (arguments: pid)

capture_packets: Watch packets crossing one network interface for a few seconds, and report tcpdump's one-line-per-packet summaries: who sent to whom, which protocol, how long, and the TCP flags. This reads packet contents on the wire - it is the one thing in this package that does - so it is gated separately and shows no payload text. Bounded by packet count, seconds and output rows. Read-only: it captures and prints, and changes nothing. (arguments: interface, packets, seconds, filter)

train.say: skip to the next song
train.positives_desc: media_control: Control music and video players: play, pause, toggle, next track, previous track, stop, restart (current track from the beginning), seek (skip ahead or go back by 'seconds'; negative goes back), or 'status' to say what is playing. (arguments: action, seconds)

negatives.desc: convert_media: Convert an audio, video or image file to another format (mp3, ogg, opus, wav, flac, m4a, mp4, webm, gif, png, jpg, webp), optionally resizing to a width. Writes a new file next to the original; never overwrites. (arguments: path, to, width)

sing: Sing a line aloud: each syllable gets its own note, on one of five named contours (rising, falling, arch, level, wave) or the real tune from a 'midi_file'. It does NOT know any song, so never present its output as a particular tune unless a MIDI file was supplied. Needs soundtouch or rubberband. (arguments: text, shape, voice_style, midi_file)

open_application: Open or launch an installed application by name or by kind, e.g. 'firefox', 'files', 'settings', 'music player', 'text editor'. Not for websites: use browse to open a site and work on it. (arguments: name)

directory_tree: Show the shape of a directory as a nested tree, with each entry's type. Use this to understand how a project or folder is laid out before opening files in it. Reports what it skipped and when it stopped early. (arguments: path, max_depth, include_hidden)

search_file_contents: Search inside text files under a directory for a literal string, and report which files contain it and on which lines. Skips binary files and very large files, and says how many it skipped. (arguments: text, path, file_pattern, case_sensitive, max_matches)

speed_test: Measure this internet connection: latency, download speed and upload speed, against Cloudflare's speed-test servers. Moves real data (default 10 MB down, 2 MB up), so it requires the 'speed-test-enabled' consent key and privacy mode off. Use for 'how fast is my internet', 'is my connection slow'. (arguments: download_mb, upload_mb)

list_shortcuts: List this machine's keyboard shortcuts, or find what one key does. Reads GNOME's two keybinding schemas, so it covers both window management and the hardware media keys, and reports that the scheme does not apply on a desktop that does not use it rather than listing defaults for a desktop that is not running. Reading a shortcut is not a change and needs no permission. (arguments: action, keys)

train.say: What is plugged in, and Thunderbolt docks.
train.positives_desc: usb_devices: What is plugged into this machine's USB ports (mice, phones, webcams, sticks, with their speed), and every Thunderbolt/USB4 device with whether it is authorised to work. Use for 'what's plugged in', 'why doesn't my dock work', 'is my webcam connected'. The USB list uses the 'usb-sense-enabled' switch. Read-only.

negatives.desc: bridge_topology: Show which network interfaces are bridges, exactly which interfaces are enslaved to each one, and which are standalone. Answers 'is this interface actually plugged into the bridge it should be', which is the usual reason a network that reported no errors carries no traffic. Read from /sys so it needs no privileges and cannot be half-applied. Reports the plumbing, not whether traffic flows. Covers this network namespace only. (arguments: bridge)

charger_info: Report what is powering this machine: on battery or plugged in, AC adapter or USB-C, whether USB Power Delivery is in use, and the charger's wattage when the firmware reports it, plus battery charge and rate.

firmware_updates: List firmware updates fwupd knows for this machine's devices (BIOS, SSD, dock, touchpad...) and what each fixes, plus the firmware versions this machine is running. Read-only; nothing is installed.

get_volume: Get the current volume and mute state of an audio output, or the default one. On a machine with more than one output - several monitors, headphones and a dock - 'the volume' is ambiguous, so pass the device exactly as `wpctl status` prints it to ask about a specific one. (arguments: device)

train.say: How much traffic each interface has carried.
train.positives_desc: interface_counters: Report how many bytes and packets each network interface has carried, in each direction, with its error and drop counters, plus the machine's TCP retransmit and error totals. Totals are since each interface came up, and the figures are read from /proc so no daemon needs to be running. Optionally sample twice to get a rate. Read-only. Counts one network namespace: an interface inside a network namespace is not visible here. (arguments: interface, sample_seconds, limit)

negatives.desc: dissect_traffic: Capture traffic on an interface and dissect it into protocol fields with tshark, Wireshark's command-line engine: which protocols are actually on the wire, and for a filter, the specific fields - TLS handshake type and SNI, DNS query names, HTTP host. This is the companion to capture_packets: that one reads packets as they cross, this one says what they are. Filters use the same grammar as both tools. Reads packet contents, so it needs the same permission as capture_packets. Writes nothing to disk. (arguments: interface, filter, packets, seconds)

bridge_topology: Show which network interfaces are bridges, exactly which interfaces are enslaved to each one, and which are standalone. Answers 'is this interface actually plugged into the bridge it should be', which is the usual reason a network that reported no errors carries no traffic. Read from /sys so it needs no privileges and cannot be half-applied. Reports the plumbing, not whether traffic flows. Covers this network namespace only. (arguments: bridge)

routing_table: Show this machine's routing table: which interface traffic leaves by, which router forwards it, and for IPv4 and IPv6 separately. Read-only, and changes nothing. (arguments: family, interface)

trace_route: Trace the network path to a host: every router along the way, how much of the traffic each one dropped, and how many milliseconds it took. Use when something specific is slow or unreachable, which is different from whether the internet works at all. (arguments: host, probes)
data_usage: How much internet data this computer has used today and this month, per network interface (from vnStat).

discover_hosts: Find which devices are on this network right now, by asking rather than by reading the cache - so devices that have never talked to this machine are found too. Reports an address and a hardware address for each, and counts devices answering on more than one address. The range is always the private network this machine is on; pass network= for a different private range, and a public one is refused. Connects to nothing it finds and reads no packet contents. Needs raw-socket access, so unprivileged it may report that rather than a partial sweep. (arguments: interface, network)

network_activity: Report what this machine's network is doing right now, per program: which processes are sending and receiving, and how fast each interface is moving. Use for 'what is using my bandwidth', 'why is the network slow', 'what is uploading', 'is something downloading right now'. Interface rates come from /proc/net/dev and always work; per-program rates need nethogs and can only name programs this user owns. Says which half it could not measure and why, and reports an unattributed socket as unattributed rather than guessing at a program. Read-only; nothing is changed or blocked.

train.say: Stopwatch.
train.positives_desc: stopwatch: A stopwatch: start, lap, read the time so far, or stop. (arguments: action)

train.say: what's in my Downloads folder?
train.positives_desc: list_directory: List the files and folders in a directory, with each one's type and size. Use this to see what is in a folder before opening, moving or deleting anything in it. (arguments: path, include_hidden)

negatives.desc: download_file: Download a file from a web address and save it to disk, reporting the size and how long it took. Use for 'download that file', 'get this installer', 'save that page'. Only http and https; a site that answers with an error page reports that rather than saving the error as if it were the file. (arguments: url, destination)

directory_tree: Show the shape of a directory as a nested tree, with each entry's type. Use this to understand how a project or folder is laid out before opening files in it. Reports what it skipped and when it stopped early. (arguments: path, max_depth, include_hidden)

empty_directories: Find directories under a path that hold nothing at all. Use for 'clean up empty folders', 'what are these leftover directories', 'tidy this up'. Empty means rmdir would succeed - a directory holding only sub-directories is not empty - and one that cannot be read is not empty either. Reports what it found and removes nothing. Read-only. (arguments: path, limit)

sync_folder: Sync one folder to another, sending only what changed - and show the plan first, before anything is copied. Use for 'copy my files to the server', 'sync these folders', 'what would change if I synced'. Does not delete anything at the destination unless you ask it to, and asks first even then. (arguments: source, destination, apply, delete)

duplicate_files: Find files with identical content under a directory, and how much space the copies waste. Use for 'why is my disk full', 'are there duplicates in my Downloads', 'where is my space going'. Reports verified groups only - same size is evidence, a matching hash is proof - and never marks one copy as the original. Read-only: it hashes and lists, and deletes nothing. (arguments: path, limit)
create_directory: Create a directory, and any missing parent directories. Succeeds without complaint if it already exists. (arguments: path)

find_files: Find files and folders by name under a directory, using a wildcard pattern such as '*.log' or 'report*'. Matches on the name only and never opens the files. To see what is in one folder, use list_directory. (arguments: pattern, path, include_hidden, max_results)

train.say: Take a photo or selfie with the webcam.
train.positives_desc: take_photo: Take a photo or selfie with the webcam and save it to the Pictures folder, optionally after a countdown in seconds (0-30). Requires the vision/camera consent. Not for screenshots (use screenshot) or video (use capture_video). (arguments: countdown, path, device, infrared)

negatives.desc: set_wallpaper: Report or change the GNOME desktop wallpaper, setting the light and dark variants together. Refuses a path that does not exist, rather than leaving a blank desktop with no error. KDE is not supported and will say so. Requires the 'appearance-control-enabled' consent key; reporting needs no such permission. (arguments: action, image)

scan_document: Scan a page and return its text (OCR), keeping the image in ~/Documents/Scans. source: 'scanner' (default; list_only lists them), 'camera' (hold the page up to the webcam; it is found and straightened), or 'photo' (straighten and read a picture of a page at path). 'Scan this letter and read it to me.' (arguments: source, path, list_only, device)

photo_video: Blur or pixelate faces, blur or remove the background, or find people and objects in a photo or video. Works by what is in it, on this computer. identify: find faces and everyday objects (people, cars, dogs, cups...); effect: blur_faces, pixelate_faces, blur_background or remove_background, saved as a new file (videos keep their sound); keyframes: save the moments a video changes; describe: say what happens in a video. For a look like sepia or sketch, or resizing and converting, use edit_image or convert_media. (arguments: action, path, effect, subject, labelled_copy)

edit_image: Edit a picture (for faces or backgrounds use photo_video) and save the result as a new file next to it: resize (width and/or height, or percent), compress (quality, or to under a size in KB), crop, upscale (2-4x), rotate, flip, grayscale, a look (sepia, vignette, sketch, paint, enhance), strip metadata (location/camera), or convert format. Several edits can be combined in one call. For effects that depend on what is in the picture (blur faces, blur the background) use photo_video. (arguments: path, width, height, percent, upscale, quality, max_kb, crop, rotate, flip, grayscale, look, strip_metadata, format)

generate_image: Make a new picture from a text description, or change a photo the way a description says (from_photo, e.g. 'make it snowy', 'as a watercolour'), drawn locally by stable-diffusion.cpp. Describe it in English. Saves a PNG and returns its path. (arguments: prompt, avoid, size, steps, seed, output, from_photo, strength)

photo_metadata: Read a photo's embedded EXIF metadata: the camera and lens, the date and time it was taken, exposure, aperture, ISO, focal length, and the GPS location if one is recorded. Use for 'when was this photo taken', 'does this picture contain my location', 'which camera took it'. JPEG and TIFF. Read-only; the file is not changed. (arguments: path)

read_image: Read a picture's basics out loud: width by height, format, and colour type, plus file size. For what the picture says, use read_document on it. The original is never modified. (arguments: path)

train.say: add 'renew passport' to my to-do list
train.positives_desc: todo_list: Keep a list of tasks that survives between turns and restarts: add an item, change its status, mark what it is blocked by, or list what is outstanding. Use this to track a multi-step job rather than holding it in the conversation. Requires the 'todo-list-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, id, content, status, blocked_by)

negatives.desc: manage_goals: Save a multi-step goal as a plan of tool steps that can be run later from the Goals panel, list saved goals, answer one that is waiting for you, or remove one. Saving runs nothing. Each step names a tool, its arguments, and a name for its result; a later step can use an earlier result as $name in a string argument, and lists the names it depends_on. A depends_on name that no earlier step produces is a question for the user: the goal waits there until they answer it. Requires the 'goals-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, goal, steps, id, answer)

manage_triggers: Arm, list, or remove automatic rules that run a Chronoa action when a perception matches - for example, notify when the battery sense reports low. A rule names one already-whitelisted skill; it cannot run an arbitrary command or an LLM-authored prompt. Listing needs no permission; arming or disarming requires the 'trigger-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, name, sense, match_mode, substring, keywords, actuator, arguments, cooldown_seconds, event_type, source, params, ask_first, retry_policy, debounce_seconds)

notes: Keep your own notes in a plain list stored on this machine: 'add' one from 'text', 'list' them, 'search' by text or id, 'remove' one by 'id'. Never sent to a model. For what the assistant itself believes and uses in its replies, use remember_fact instead. (arguments: action, text, query, id)

reminders: A dated list of reminders you can keep coming back to: add one, list what is still due, mark one done, or remove one. Optionally with a due time in words, e.g. 'tomorrow 9am' or 'in 3 hours'. (arguments: action, number, text, due)

set_timer: Set a countdown timer that sends a desktop notification when it finishes; list pending timers, say how much time is left, add or take off time, pause, resume, reset to the original length, and cancel. With one timer pending, 'my timer' needs no id. The countdown is owned by systemd, so it fires even if the assistant is closed. It is refused rather than silently accepted when systemd is unavailable, because a timer recorded as pending that will never fire is the same lie as a camera reported as disabled when it is not. (arguments: action, seconds, label, id)
lab_network_list: List the isolated lab networks built on this machine, with their subnets. Read-only.

list_apps: List the applications installed on this machine, optionally filtered by a search term, so a request to open something can be answered with what actually exists rather than a guess. (arguments: search)

train.say: Temperatures and fan speeds.
train.positives_desc: temperatures: Current CPU, GPU, disk and board temperatures, fan speeds and fan control, read from the kernel's hardware sensors. Use for 'is my laptop overheating', 'how hot is the CPU', 'how fast is the fan'. Uses the 'hwmon-sense-enabled' switch. Read-only.

negatives.desc: cpu_frequency: What the processor is doing right now: which speed governor it is in, roughly what speed it is running at, and the range its hardware allows. Use after setting a power mode, to see whether the machine actually took it up - 'why is my fan so loud', 'is my CPU being throttled', 'did performance mode do anything'. Read-only; changes nothing.

system_history: What this machine's CPU, disk, memory or paging was doing earlier, from the sysstat accounting records rather than a live reading. Use for 'was this busy last night', 'what was using the disk at lunchtime', 'why was the fan loud earlier'. Says plainly when no history has been recorded, because that is not the same as the machine having been idle. Read-only. (arguments: topic)

train.say: What this machine can actually do.
train.positives_desc: machine_capabilities: Report what this machine can actually do: which of the commands Chronoa knows how to use are really present, which Python modules import here, and which services are enabled. Asks the live machine rather than reading the shipped inventory, which describes the image it was built from and not necessarily this one. Use it before offering to convert a file, edit an image, read a document or capture audio, to find out whether that is even possible here.

negatives.desc: backup_status: Whether this machine's files are actually backed up off it: how many restic snapshots exist, when the most recent was taken, what it covered, and whether the repository still passes restic's own integrity check. Use for 'is my backup working', 'when did I last back up', 'do I have a copy of my files'. A machine with no repository configured says so plainly, because that means there is no backup. Read-only: it never writes to the repository. (arguments: repository)

calculate: Evaluate arithmetic and percentages ('15% of 2400'), or convert between units. Handles the four operations, powers, parentheses, factorial, permutations and combinations (perm/nPr, comb/nCr), gcd, lcm, sqrt, exp, log, ln, trig and inverse trig, and pi/e/tau - exact for whole numbers. For algebra with variables, derivatives, integrals, limits or equations, use solve_math. Converts length, mass, volume, time, data, pressure, frequency, power, energy and temperature, in the units a person actually meets - say '200 km to miles' or '70kg in lb'. Runs entirely on this machine with no network call. Refuses to guess: a percentage needs a number to apply to, and converting between quantities that measure different things is an error rather than a number. (arguments: expression)

compression_savings: How much space btrfs compression is saving on this machine: the uncompressed size of the data, how much disk it actually occupies, and which compressor is doing it. Use for 'how much is compression saving me', 'why is my disk less full than the files suggest'. Read-only; nothing is changed.

cpu_frequency: What the processor is doing right now: which speed governor it is in, roughly what speed it is running at, and the range its hardware allows. Use after setting a power mode, to see whether the machine actually took it up - 'why is my fan so loud', 'is my CPU being throttled', 'did performance mode do anything'. Read-only; changes nothing.

lab_network_create: Build an isolated lab network on this machine: a network namespace holding a bridge, with named subnets in namespaces of their own. A public subnet can reach the internet through the uplink; a private one can reach this network and nothing beyond it. Returns the exact plan and changes nothing unless apply=true, which needs your system password. (arguments: name, cidr, subnets, internet, apply)

list_apps: List the applications installed on this machine, optionally filtered by a search term, so a request to open something can be answered with what actually exists rather than a guess. (arguments: search)

list_fonts: List the font families installed on this machine (optionally only those whose name contains some text), and which real font the generic names - sans-serif, serif, monospace, emoji - or a font you name actually resolve to. Use for 'what fonts do I have', 'is Fira Code installed', 'which font is used for monospace'. Read-only. (arguments: query)

train.say: Open the system Settings at a page.
train.positives_desc: open_settings: Open the system Settings app at a specific page, e.g. 'wifi', 'bluetooth', 'display', 'sound', 'power', 'privacy', 'keyboard', 'mouse', 'touchpad', 'printers', 'users', 'about', 'date_time', 'region', 'notifications', 'background', 'accessibility'. GNOME and KDE Plasma. Use open_application for Settings without a page. (arguments: page)

negatives.desc: open_application: Open or launch an installed application by name or by kind, e.g. 'firefox', 'files', 'settings', 'music player', 'text editor'. Not for websites: use browse to open a site and work on it. (arguments: name)

watch: Your MoYoung/Da Fit smartwatch: 'summary' (steps, distance, calories for 3 days, last night's sleep stages, today's stress, workouts), 'measure' a heart rate, blood oxygen or blood pressure on the wrist (takes up to a minute), read 'settings', 'set' one (step_goal, time_format 12h/24h, units metric/imperial, raise_to_wake, sedentary_reminder, other_app_notifications, power_saving, heart_rate_auto_interval, do_not_disturb '22:00-07:00'), 'sync_time', 'notify' (show a message on the watch), or set the 'profile' (height, weight, age, gender - weight is never measured by the watch). Requires the 'bluetooth-gatt-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, device, what, setting, value, sender, text, kind, height_cm, weight_kg, age, gender)

open_file: Open one specific file or folder (by its path) using the desktop's default application for it - the same thing double-clicking it would do. To launch an app such as the file manager, use open_application. (arguments: path)

open_files: Find which programs have a file, directory or network socket open. Use for 'what is using this file', 'why can't I delete this', 'what has my disk open', 'which process is holding that socket'. Names the holding program with its full command line, and flags deleted files whose space cannot be reclaimed. Reads only this user's processes unless run as root. Read-only: it lists open handles and never closes one. (arguments: path, pid, limit)

system_history: What this machine's CPU, disk, memory or paging was doing earlier, from the sysstat accounting records rather than a live reading. Use for 'was this busy last night', 'what was using the disk at lunchtime', 'why was the fan loud earlier'. Says plainly when no history has been recorded, because that is not the same as the machine having been idle. Read-only. (arguments: topic)

system_info: Describe the machine Chronoa is running on: distribution, kernel, architecture, uptime, load, memory, CPU count, whether this is a desktop session or a container, and the hardware identity (make, model, board, BIOS version).

browse: Open a website and do things on it for the person: find information, fill in forms, click through. Drive a web browser: navigate, read the page's text (get_text), click, type, select options, scroll, move through history, take screenshots and wait for conditions. While Chronoa's window is open this is the in-app browser the user can watch: there it opens only http(s) pages the egress policy allows, and key, hover, drag, upload_file, tabs and evaluate are not available. Otherwise it is a headless Chromium with all actions. Requires the web sense to be enabled and privacy mode to be off. (arguments: action, url, selector, text, key, value, label, files, x, y, to_x, to_y, to_selector, delta_x, delta_y, steps, repeat, tab_id, path, wait_for, timeout, settle)

train.say: Read that back to me
