Use this to find what is using the machine - pass sort_by='memory' for the RAM question, which CPU order does not answer - or the pid of something you want to stop. (arguments: name_filter, sort_by, limit)

machine_capabilities: Report what this machine can actually do: which of the commands Chronoa knows how to use are really present, which Python modules import here, and which services are enabled. Asks the live machine rather than reading the shipped inventory, which describes the image it was built from and not necessarily this one. Use it before offering to convert a file, edit an image, read a document or capture audio, to find out whether that is even possible here.

manage_triggers: Arm, list, or remove automatic rules that run a Chronoa action when a perception matches - for example, notify when the battery sense reports low. A rule names one already-whitelisted skill; it cannot run an arbitrary command or an LLM-authored prompt. Listing needs no permission; arming or disarming requires the 'trigger-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, name, sense, match_mode, substring, keywords, actuator, arguments, cooldown_seconds, event_type, source, params, ask_first, retry_policy, debounce_seconds)

train.say: Read what is on your calendar.
train.positives_desc: calendar_events: List events on the user's calendars (GNOME calendars and online accounts): today, tomorrow, this week, or the next few hours. Requires the 'calendar-read-enabled' consent key. (arguments: range, hours)

negatives.desc: calendar_month: Show the calendar for a month (default this month), with today marked. (arguments: month, year)

calendar_edit: Change the user's calendar: 'create' adds an event to the default calendar (title, start, optional duration or end, location); 'move' reschedules an event found by its current time and/or title to new_start; 'cancel' deletes one. Times in words: 'tomorrow 3pm', 'friday 5 pm', '2026-10-09 14:00'. Move and cancel ask the person to confirm. Ambiguous matches are refused with the candidates. Requires the 'calendar-write-enabled' consent key (move/cancel also 'calendar-read-enabled'). No invitations are sent. (arguments: action, title, start, duration, end, new_start, location, notes)

manage_triggers: Arm, list, or remove automatic rules that run a Chronoa action when a perception matches - for example, notify when the battery sense reports low. A rule names one already-whitelisted skill; it cannot run an arbitrary command or an LLM-authored prompt. Listing needs no permission; arming or disarming requires the 'trigger-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, name, sense, match_mode, substring, keywords, actuator, arguments, cooldown_seconds, event_type, source, params, ask_first, retry_policy, debounce_seconds)
data_usage: How much internet data this computer has used today and this month, per network interface (from vnStat).

date_math: Date arithmetic: days until a date ('how many days until 25 December'), the date N days/weeks/months from a date ('what date is 45 days from now'), days between two dates, or the weekday of a date. (arguments: operation, date, other_date, amount, unit)

set_locale: Report the system language and regional formats, list the locales available on this machine, or change one: the system language, or the date format (British day/month or American month/day order), number format (decimal comma or point), money, measurement or paper size (e.g. what='dates', locale='en_GB.UTF-8'). Takes effect at the next login. Changing requires the 'locale-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, locale, what)

routines: Save a routine: a short phrase (e.g. 'good morning', 'leaving work') that later runs a whole request, e.g. 'tell me the weather, my calendar today and the top news'. Also list or delete routines. Saving runs nothing; saying the phrase later runs the request. (arguments: action, name, request, phrases)

train.say: Check what a lab network can actually reach.
train.positives_desc: lab_network_status: What a lab network can actually reach: a real ping from inside each subnet, not just what the routing table says. (arguments: name)

negatives.desc: lab_network_create: Build an isolated lab network on this machine: a network namespace holding a bridge, with named subnets in namespaces of their own. A public subnet can reach the internet through the uplink; a private one can reach this network and nothing beyond it. Returns the exact plan and changes nothing unless apply=true, which needs your system password. (arguments: name, cidr, subnets, internet, apply)
lab_network_destroy: Remove a lab network built by lab_network_create, and everything in it. Only ever removes networks this tool built. Returns the plan unless apply=true. (arguments: name, apply)
lab_network_list: List the isolated lab networks built on this machine, with their subnets. Read-only.
check_internet: Check whether the internet is working and, if not, which step fails: network connection, router, internet, DNS, or websites. Also reports the delay to the router and to the internet.

check_port: Check whether a specific port on a specific host accepts connections from this machine, and say why it does not - refused (the host is up, nothing is listening), timed out (a firewall, or a host that is off), or the name does not resolve. Use for 'is my server reachable', 'why can nothing connect to it', 'is port 443 open on that box'. Opens exactly one connection and sends nothing; it is not a scan. (arguments: host, port)

check_units: Check whether systemd unit files are valid and say what is wrong with them - a missing ExecStart binary, an unknown key, a dependency that does not exist - by running systemd-analyze verify on just the units you name. With no unit named, lists the services this machine has. This is a static check of the file: it does not know whether a dependency is down or a path is mounted, so a clean report does not promise the service will start. Reading only; nothing is started, stopped or changed. (arguments: unit)
check_updates: Check whether this machine has package updates waiting, without installing anything and without needing root. Works on Arch and other pacman systems.

train.say: Read or change a desktop setting (animations, clock, cursor, touchpad...).
train.positives_desc: desktop_setting: Read or change one desktop setting from a fixed list: animations (window and menu animations); cursor_size (mouse pointer size in pixels (24 is normal; 32, 48, 64 are larger)); single_click (open files and folders with a single click); clock_24h (show the top-bar clock in 24-hour format); clock_seconds (show seconds in the top-bar clock); battery_percentage (show the battery percentage in the top bar); hot_corner (open the overview when the pointer hits the top-left corner); natural_scroll (touchpad natural (reverse) scrolling); tap_to_click (tap the touchpad to click). Changing requires the 'appearance-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: setting, value)

negatives.desc: alarm: Alarm clock: set an alarm at a time of day (once, or repeating daily/weekdays/weekends/chosen days), list alarms, say when the next one is, change one's time or label, snooze the one that just rang, or delete one. Examples: 'set an alarm for 7am', 'alarm for 6:30 on weekdays', 'when is my next alarm?', 'change my 7am alarm to 7:30', 'snooze', 'delete the 7am alarm'. Times may be words ('7am', '7:30 pm', 'tomorrow 6:45'). It rings with a notification and the alarm sound even if the assistant is closed; it is held by systemd --user, so a reboot drops it until alarms are next listed, which re-arms it. (arguments: action, time, label, repeat, id, new_time, new_label, minutes)

set_scaling: Report or change the desktop's text scaling factor (1.0 is normal, 1.5 is 150%). Text scaling only - display-resolution and HiDPI scaling are not changed by this, because driving those black-screens sessions. Requires the 'appearance-control-enabled' consent key; reporting needs no such permission. (arguments: action, factor)

set_theme: Report or change whether the desktop uses a light or dark appearance, on GNOME or KDE. Reports the applied theme separately from the preference, because setting the preference does not make every application follow it. Requires the 'appearance-control-enabled' consent key; reporting needs no such permission. (arguments: action)

set_wallpaper: Report or change the GNOME desktop wallpaper, setting the light and dark variants together. Refuses a path that does not exist, rather than leaving a blank desktop with no error. KDE is not supported and will say so. Requires the 'appearance-control-enabled' consent key; reporting needs no such permission. (arguments: action, image)

ui_elements: Use another app's controls by what they are, through the accessibility tree. apps: which apps are reachable. inspect: list a window's buttons, fields, menus and labels with ids (app = its name; query narrows by text). press: activate an element by id (a button, checkbox, link, menu item). set_text: put text in a field by id. read: an element's text or value. menu: open a menu path like 'File > Export'. drive: one turn of driving - give an action and a control number and the reply is the app's new state in the same short numbered form, which is what a small model can act on. act: click, type or key an app by name or position, with a visible cursor. state: the numbered controls an app is showing. Works on a container's app and on this desktop's own apps alike. Requires 'input-control-enabled'; drive start also runs a container, so it needs 'container-control-enabled' as well. (arguments: action, app, id, text, query, path, do, how, number, image, keys, x, y)

set_timer: Set a countdown timer that sends a desktop notification when it finishes; list pending timers, say how much time is left, add or take off time, pause, resume, reset to the original length, and cancel. With one timer pending, 'my timer' needs no id. The countdown is owned by systemd, so it fires even if the assistant is closed. It is refused rather than silently accepted when systemd is unavailable, because a timer recorded as pending that will never fire is the same lie as a camera reported as disabled when it is not. (arguments: action, seconds, label, id)

set_locale: Report the system language and regional formats, list the locales available on this machine, or change one: the system language, or the date format (British day/month or American month/day order), number format (decimal comma or point), money, measurement or paper size (e.g. what='dates', locale='en_GB.UTF-8'). Takes effect at the next login. Changing requires the 'locale-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, locale, what)

train.say: what's using the most CPU right now?
train.positives_desc: list_processes: List the processes running on this machine, with their pid, name, owner, CPU and memory use, sorted by CPU unless sort_by says otherwise. Use this to find what is using the machine - pass sort_by='memory' for the RAM question, which CPU order does not answer - or the pid of something you want to stop. (arguments: name_filter, sort_by, limit)

negatives.desc: cpu_frequency: What the processor is doing right now: which speed governor it is in, roughly what speed it is running at, and the range its hardware allows. Use after setting a power mode, to see whether the machine actually took it up - 'why is my fan so loud', 'is my CPU being throttled', 'did performance mode do anything'. Read-only; changes nothing.

cpu_per_core: Which individual processor cores are busy right now, and how much of each is user time versus waiting on disk. Use when the machine feels slow but nothing looks busy - a single process pinning one core looks idle in every system-wide average. Read-only; starts nothing.

process_cost: What each running program is COSTING this machine right now, measured over the last second rather than as a snapshot: percent CPU split into user and system time, how much memory it holds, page faults (including the major ones that mean it is thrashing), and how many kB a second it is reading and writing. Answers 'what is using my CPU', 'what is making my computer slow', 'what is writing to my disk all the time', 'which program is swapping', 'why did everything freeze'. Use this when the machine feels slow; use list_processes to see what is running and disk_activity to see whether the disk itself is busy. Read-only; nothing is started, stopped or changed.

thread_activity: Show the individual THREADS of a process - or of the whole machine - with the CPU each is using right now and the kernel function it is blocked in. Use for 'which thread is using the CPU', 'this program is at 300 percent', 'what is this thread waiting on', 'why is this stuck', 'which of these threads is busy'. Goes one level below process_detail and list_processes, which report one figure for the whole process and cannot tell a program with one hot thread from one using every core evenly. Read-only; nothing is sampled with a tool, attached to or changed. (arguments: pid)

system_history: What this machine's CPU, disk, memory or paging was doing earlier, from the sysstat accounting records rather than a live reading. Use for 'was this busy last night', 'what was using the disk at lunchtime', 'why was the fan loud earlier'. Says plainly when no history has been recorded, because that is not the same as the machine having been idle. Read-only. (arguments: topic)

network_activity: Report what this machine's network is doing right now, per program: which processes are sending and receiving, and how fast each interface is moving. Use for 'what is using my bandwidth', 'why is the network slow', 'what is uploading', 'is something downloading right now'. Interface rates come from /proc/net/dev and always work; per-program rates need nethogs and can only name programs this user owns. Says which half it could not measure and why, and reports an unattributed socket as unattributed rather than guessing at a program. Read-only; nothing is changed or blocked.
click_pointer: Click a mouse button at the current pointer position. Requires the 'input-control-enabled' consent key (separate from the vision sense) to be enabled. (arguments: button, count)

train.say: Find a place, get directions, or look up what is nearby.
train.positives_desc: maps: OpenStreetMap maps: find where a place is ('find'), driving/walking/cycling directions ('directions') or just distance and time ('travel_time') between places, the nearest kind of place such as petrol pump, hotel, ATM or hospital ('nearby'), or open a place or route on the map in the browser ('open'). Times are typical, without live traffic. With no origin, 'here' is this computer's location. Requires the web sense and privacy mode off; 'here' also needs the location sense. (arguments: action, place, destination, origin, mode, what, near, limit)

negatives.desc: find_and_replace: Find a string across files under a directory and optionally replace it. Reports what it would change without changing anything unless dry_run is explicitly false. Requires the 'bulk-edit-enabled' consent key. (arguments: find, replace, path, file_pattern, dry_run, case_sensitive)

search_documents: Search inside the user's files by their contents, using the desktop's own search index (LocalSearch on GNOME, Baloo on Plasma). Requires the 'document-search-enabled' consent key. (arguments: query, kind, limit)

search_file_contents: Search inside text files under a directory for a literal string, and report which files contain it and on which lines. Skips binary files and very large files, and says how many it skipped. (arguments: text, path, file_pattern, case_sensitive, max_matches)

search_my_files: Search your own files by meaning - documents, notes, code - in a directory you choose, or your home if you name none. 'search': what matches a few words. 'reindex': read the directory and build or refresh the index (needed before the first search). 'status': what would be indexed and whether this machine can search by meaning. Needs the 'file-index-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, query, path, limit)

web_search: Look something up on the web and return what the pages actually say: facts, prices, how-tos, anything no more specific tool covers. Give a search query, a specific URL, or both. For a scholarly question - a paper, a preprint, prior work, 'what does the research say' - set source=arxiv and it searches the arXiv preprint archive instead of the web. For news headlines use news; to click, fill in or book something on a site use browse. Requires the web sense to be enabled and privacy mode to be off. (arguments: query, url, source)

find_files: Find files and folders by name under a directory, using a wildcard pattern such as '*.log' or 'report*'. Matches on the name only and never opens the files. To see what is in one folder, use list_directory. (arguments: pattern, path, include_hidden, max_results)

find_recently_modified: List files under a directory whose recorded modification time is within the last N days, newest first. Use this to answer 'what did I change today'. This is a timestamp, so a tool that preserves or sets times (tar, rsync, cp -p) can move an entry without the content changing. (arguments: path, within_days, pattern, limit)

train.say: Encode or decode text.
train.positives_desc: encode_text: Encode or decode text: base64, url (percent-encoding), hex, binary, rot13, morse. (arguments: text, scheme, direction)

negatives.desc: ir_remote: Send and receive infrared remote-control codes, and build or read the pulse-space timings themselves. 'devices': is there IR hardware here (most machines have none, and that is a true answer). 'encode': turn an address and command into the NEC or RC-6 timings that would carry them. 'decode': turn timings into a code. 'send': transmit a code through an IR device. 'receive': capture a button press and decode it. Needs the 'ir-remote-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, protocol, address, command, timings, seconds)

fm_radio: FM and AM broadcast radio. Five actions: 'hardware' for whether this computer can receive anything at all (a laptop usually cannot, and that is a true answer rather than a failure - it needs an RTL2832U USB dongle), 'bands' for the coverage, 'tune' to a frequency, 'decode' to demodulate a recorded IQ capture, and 'scan' to look for carriers in one. A frequency is given in MHz, e.g. 98.6. rtl_fm is narrowband and retunes per channel, so it cannot scan - scanning needs a wideband recording. No station names are guessed: a carrier gives a frequency, and naming it would need a table for your region. Requires the 'fm-radio-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, frequency, seconds, file, centre_mhz, out, deemphasis_us)
type_text: Type text at the currently focused window. Requires the 'input-control-enabled' consent key (separate from the vision sense) to be enabled. (arguments: text)
read_text_file: Read a text file and return its contents, optionally a range of lines. Use this to see what a file actually says. (arguments: path, start_line, max_lines)

translate_text: Translate text into another language, using a local translation tool when one is installed and a web service otherwise. The reply says which was used, because one sends your text to a third party. (arguments: text, to_language, from_language)

write_text_file: Write text to a file, creating it or replacing its contents. Refuses to replace a non-empty file unless asked to overwrite, and refuses binary data. (arguments: path, content, overwrite, append)

qr_code: read: decode every QR code and barcode in a picture (path) or on the screen (screen=true, needs the vision consent). create: make a QR code PNG of text (a URL, Wi-Fi details, a note) at output. (arguments: action, path, screen, text, output)

train.say: Convert audio, video and pictures.
train.positives_desc: convert_media: Convert an audio, video or image file to another format (mp3, ogg, opus, wav, flac, m4a, mp4, webm, gif, png, jpg, webp), optionally resizing to a width. Writes a new file next to the original; never overwrites. (arguments: path, to, width)

negatives.desc: photo_video: Blur or pixelate faces, blur or remove the background, or find people and objects in a photo or video. Works by what is in it, on this computer. identify: find faces and everyday objects (people, cars, dogs, cups...); effect: blur_faces, pixelate_faces, blur_background or remove_background, saved as a new file (videos keep their sound); keyframes: save the moments a video changes; describe: say what happens in a video. For a look like sepia or sketch, or resizing and converting, use edit_image or convert_media. (arguments: action, path, effect, subject, labelled_copy)

media_control: Control music and video players: play, pause, toggle, next track, previous track, stop, restart (current track from the beginning), seek (skip ahead or go back by 'seconds'; negative goes back), or 'status' to say what is playing. (arguments: action, seconds)

create_video: Create a video: a slideshow from a list of pictures (each shown for a few seconds), or a simple clip of a colour for a duration. Writes a new .mp4 next to the inputs; never overwrites. (arguments: images, seconds, color, duration, width)

edit_audio: Edit a sound file and save the result as a new file next to it (never overwriting the original): trim between times, raise or lower the volume, normalize loudness, change speed, or convert to an audio format. End times accept seconds or 'MM:SS'/'HH:MM:SS'. (arguments: path, start, end, volume, normalize, speed, to)

edit_video: Edit a video and save the result as a new file next to it (never overwriting the original): trim between times, resize to a width, rotate, mute or keep only the audio, or change the speed. End times accept seconds ('95'), or 'MM:SS' / 'HH:MM:SS'. (arguments: path, start, end, width, rotate, mute, audio_only, speed, output)

read_video: Read a video's basics out loud (for subtitles or what was said use recording): how long it is, its resolution, its video codec, whether it has audio, and its bitrate. Add keyframes=true to also save the moments the image changes. The original is never modified. (arguments: path, keyframes)

search_documents: Search inside the user's files by their contents, using the desktop's own search index (LocalSearch on GNOME, Baloo on Plasma). Requires the 'document-search-enabled' consent key. (arguments: query, kind, limit)

held_out.positives_desc: random_pick: Flip a coin, roll dice ('2d6'), pick a random number in a range, or choose one of a list of options. (arguments: kind, dice, low, high, options)

negatives.desc: edit_image: Edit a picture (for faces or backgrounds use photo_video) and save the result as a new file next to it: resize (width and/or height, or percent), compress (quality, or to under a size in KB), crop, upscale (2-4x), rotate, flip, grayscale, a look (sepia, vignette, sketch, paint, enhance), strip metadata (location/camera), or convert format. Several edits can be combined in one call. For effects that depend on what is in the picture (blur faces, blur the background) use photo_video. (arguments: path, width, height, percent, upscale, quality, max_kb, crop, rotate, flip, grayscale, look, strip_metadata, format)
generate_password: Generate a strong random password, or a passphrase of random words, and copy it to the clipboard (it is never said or shown in the reply). (arguments: kind, length, symbols)

held_out.positives_desc: set_theme: Report or change whether the desktop uses a light or dark appearance, on GNOME or KDE. Reports the applied theme separately from the preference, because setting the preference does not make every application follow it. Requires the 'appearance-control-enabled' consent key; reporting needs no such permission. (arguments: action)

negatives.desc: airplane_mode: Report which radios (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, mobile broadband) are on, or turn airplane mode on (all radios off) or off. Changing requires the 'radio-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action)

browse: Open a website and do things on it for the person: find information, fill in forms, click through. Drive a web browser: navigate, read the page's text (get_text), click, type, select options, scroll, move through history, take screenshots and wait for conditions. While Chronoa's window is open this is the in-app browser the user can watch: there it opens only http(s) pages the egress policy allows, and key, hover, drag, upload_file, tabs and evaluate are not available. Otherwise it is a headless Chromium with all actions. Requires the web sense to be enabled and privacy mode to be off. (arguments: action, url, selector, text, key, value, label, files, x, y, to_x, to_y, to_selector, delta_x, delta_y, steps, repeat, tab_id, path, wait_for, timeout, settle)

toggle_wifi: Turn the Wi-Fi radio on or off (only Wi-Fi - airplane_mode switches every radio, connect_wifi joins a network), or report whether Wi-Fi is on. Changing requires the 'radio-control-enabled' consent key; status needs no permission. (arguments: action)

set_wallpaper: Report or change the GNOME desktop wallpaper, setting the light and dark variants together. Refuses a path that does not exist, rather than leaving a blank desktop with no error. KDE is not supported and will say so. Requires the 'appearance-control-enabled' consent key; reporting needs no such permission. (arguments: action, image)

convert_currency: Convert an amount of money between currencies (rupees, dollars, euros, pounds, yen, ...) at today's ECB reference rate. Requires the web sense and privacy mode off. (arguments: amount, from_currency, to_currency)

cpu_frequency: What the processor is doing right now: which speed governor it is in, roughly what speed it is running at, and the range its hardware allows. Use after setting a power mode, to see whether the machine actually took it up - 'why is my fan so loud', 'is my CPU being throttled', 'did performance mode do anything'. Read-only; changes nothing.

dns_lookup: Look a hostname or address up in DNS and report what came back: the addresses, or the mail servers, name servers, TXT records, certificate records or other records a name publishes, and whether the answer is DNSSEC-signed and valid. Distinguishes 'this name does not exist' from 'the resolver did not answer', because those have different fixes. Obeys privacy mode, since the query goes to a resolver outside this machine. Read-only. (arguments: name, type)

held_out.positives_desc: list_containers: List this machine's containers: distroboxes (by name, with their image and whether they are running) and podman/docker containers, including any that exited because they ran out of memory, plus how much disk the images use. Use for 'what distroboxes do I have', 'is my container running', 'why did my container die'. The podman details use the 'containers-sense-enabled' switch. Read-only.

negatives.desc: container: Run containers on this machine with podman (run an image, run a command inside a running container, stop it, read its logs, list what is running, list local images, pull one) and start/stop nspawn machines with machinectl. A container started with display=x11 draws on this desktop, and the ui_elements tool is what drives it by name with a visible cursor; this tool starts it, and stops it. Needs 'container-control-enabled', off by default. (arguments: action, image, name, command, detach, display, share_bus, publish, all, tail)

explain_command: Explain a Linux shell command (not a general topic) from the local manuals (tldr, man), e.g. 'what does tar do', 'how do I use rsync'; or find which command does something, e.g. 'which command shows disk usage'. (arguments: command, task)

manage_triggers: Arm, list, or remove automatic rules that run a Chronoa action when a perception matches - for example, notify when the battery sense reports low. A rule names one already-whitelisted skill; it cannot run an arbitrary command or an LLM-authored prompt. Listing needs no permission; arming or disarming requires the 'trigger-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, name, sense, match_mode, substring, keywords, actuator, arguments, cooldown_seconds, event_type, source, params, ask_first, retry_policy, debounce_seconds)

ui_elements: Use another app's controls by what they are, through the accessibility tree. apps: which apps are reachable. inspect: list a window's buttons, fields, menus and labels with ids (app = its name; query narrows by text). press: activate an element by id (a button, checkbox, link, menu item). set_text: put text in a field by id. read: an element's text or value. menu: open a menu path like 'File > Export'. drive: one turn of driving - give an action and a control number and the reply is the app's new state in the same short numbered form, which is what a small model can act on. act: click, type or key an app by name or position, with a visible cursor. state: the numbered controls an app is showing. Works on a container's app and on this desktop's own apps alike. Requires 'input-control-enabled'; drive start also runs a container, so it needs 'container-control-enabled' as well. (arguments: action, app, id, text, query, path, do, how, number, image, keys, x, y)

edit_image: Edit a picture (for faces or backgrounds use photo_video) and save the result as a new file next to it: resize (width and/or height, or percent), compress (quality, or to under a size in KB), crop, upscale (2-4x), rotate, flip, grayscale, a look (sepia, vignette, sketch, paint, enhance), strip metadata (location/camera), or convert format. Several edits can be combined in one call. For effects that depend on what is in the picture (blur faces, blur the background) use photo_video. (arguments: path, width, height, percent, upscale, quality, max_kb, crop, rotate, flip, grayscale, look, strip_metadata, format)

generate_image: Make a new picture from a text description, or change a photo the way a description says (from_photo, e.g. 'make it snowy', 'as a watercolour'), drawn locally by stable-diffusion.cpp. Describe it in English. Saves a PNG and returns its path. (arguments: prompt, avoid, size, steps, seed, output, from_photo, strength)

read_image: Read a picture's basics out loud: width by height, format, and colour type, plus file size. For what the picture says, use read_document on it. The original is never modified. (arguments: path)

held_out.say: Remove a lab network this machine built.
held_out.positives_desc: lab_network_destroy: Remove a lab network built by lab_network_create, and everything in it. Only ever removes networks this tool built. Returns the plan unless apply=true. (arguments: name, apply)

negatives.desc: lab_network_list: List the isolated lab networks built on this machine, with their subnets. Read-only.

lab_network_create: Build an isolated lab network on this machine: a network namespace holding a bridge, with named subnets in namespaces of their own. A public subnet can reach the internet through the uplink; a private one can reach this network and nothing beyond it. Returns the exact plan and changes nothing unless apply=true, which needs your system password. (arguments: name, cidr, subnets, internet, apply)
lab_network_status: What a lab network can actually reach: a real ping from inside each subnet, not just what the routing table says. (arguments: name)

machine_capabilities: Report what this machine can actually do: which of the commands Chronoa knows how to use are really present, which Python modules import here, and which services are enabled. Asks the live machine rather than reading the shipped inventory, which describes the image it was built from and not necessarily this one. Use it before offering to convert a file, edit an image, read a document or capture audio, to find out whether that is even possible here.

list_wifi_networks: Scan for and list the WiFi networks in range, with signal strength and whether this machine is joined to one. Scans the radio, so it requires the 'network-sense-enabled' consent. (arguments: rescan)

network_activity: Report what this machine's network is doing right now, per program: which processes are sending and receiving, and how fast each interface is moving. Use for 'what is using my bandwidth', 'why is the network slow', 'what is uploading', 'is something downloading right now'. Interface rates come from /proc/net/dev and always work; per-program rates need nethogs and can only name programs this user owns. Says which half it could not measure and why, and reports an unattributed socket as unattributed rather than guessing at a program. Read-only; nothing is changed or blocked.

scan_network: Find which devices are on the local network, with their names, addresses and hardware vendors. Local addresses only. Requires the network sense to be enabled. (arguments: range, resolve_names)

held_out.say: Mute or unmute the microphone input.
held_out.positives_desc: set_mic_mute: Mute or unmute the default microphone input, or report whether it is currently muted. Output volume is a separate skill. Requires the 'mic-control-enabled' consent key; reporting needs no such permission. (arguments: action)

negatives.desc: set_privacy: Control the machine's privacy: mute or unmute the microphone, enable or disable a camera, or blank the screen. Muting the microphone is a user-level stream mute that any new application can override, and the reply says so rather than implying the hardware is off. Disabling a camera needs root and is only possible on drivers that expose a disable control, so a device with no such control is reported as unsupported rather than disabled. Blanking works on X11; under Wayland it would need a permission prompt, so the idle timeout is offered instead. Every action says how to undo it. (arguments: action, device)
set_mute: Mute or unmute the sound from the speakers or headphones ('mute the sound', 'unmute'). The microphone is set_mic_mute. (arguments: mute, device)

audio_output: List the speakers/headphones (outputs) and microphones (inputs) and which one is the default, or switch the default output or input - 'play through my headphones', 'use the USB microphone', 'send sound to the HDMI monitor'. Pick a device by its number or part of its name. (arguments: action, device, kind)

phone_remote: Press keys on the paired phone as a Bluetooth keyboard: 'press' the camera 'shutter' (takes a photo in the camera app), play_pause, next, previous, volume_up/down, mute; or 'type' text into whatever field is focused on the phone. The phone must have paired 'Chronoa Remote'. Requires the 'phone-remote-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, key, text)

edit_video: Edit a video and save the result as a new file next to it (never overwriting the original): trim between times, resize to a width, rotate, mute or keep only the audio, or change the speed. End times accept seconds ('95'), or 'MM:SS' / 'HH:MM:SS'. (arguments: path, start, end, width, rotate, mute, audio_only, speed, output)

get_volume: Get the current volume and mute state of an audio output, or the default one. On a machine with more than one output - several monitors, headphones and a dock - 'the volume' is ambiguous, so pass the device exactly as `wpctl status` prints it to ask about a specific one. (arguments: device)

bluetooth_call: Use a paired Android phone as a Bluetooth speakerphone, with no cable and no app on the phone. 'status' says whether a phone is connected as a hands-free unit, whether a call is in progress, and which audio profile its call audio arrived on. 'dial' places a call - 'dial number="+441234567890"' - asking you to confirm first, because it rings someone. 'answer' and 'hangup' work on a call already in progress. 'audio' reports where the call's voice is going and names anything missing from that path, and 'profile' switches the card between wide-band hfp_hf and narrow-band hsp_hs. The phone stays the radio; this routes the voice to this computer's speakers and microphone. Needs the phone connected over Bluetooth, not merely paired, and the 'bluetooth-call-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, card, profile, to, number)

held_out.positives_desc: read_logs: Read recent log output from a named system service, or from the kernel when no service is named. Returns the most recent lines first-context-last, and says how much it did not show. (arguments: unit, lines, priority, since)

negatives.desc: log_files: See which log files under /var/log are largest, whether they are still being written to right now, and whether anything rotates them. Use for 'why is my disk full', 'what is filling up the disk', 'is that log growing'. Also reports logrotate configuration errors, which silently stop a rotation. Read-only: it runs logrotate in debug mode, which rotates nothing. (arguments: limit)

system_history: What this machine's CPU, disk, memory or paging was doing earlier, from the sysstat accounting records rather than a live reading. Use for 'was this busy last night', 'what was using the disk at lunchtime', 'why was the fan loud earlier'. Says plainly when no history has been recorded, because that is not the same as the machine having been idle. Read-only. (arguments: topic)

system_info: Describe the machine Chronoa is running on: distribution, kernel, architecture, uptime, load, memory, CPU count, whether this is a desktop session or a container, and the hardware identity (make, model, board, BIOS version).
cleanup_report: Report what could be cleaned up to free disk space - trash, caches, the system log, unused Flatpak runtimes - with sizes. Reads only; deletes nothing.

cleanup_apply: Actually free the disk space cleanup_report measured: empty your cache folder, or remove Flatpak runtimes no app uses. Both are recoverable or provably unused. Requires the 'cleanup-enabled' consent key. The system log is not here - that needs root, which Chronoa cannot ask for from inside a tool call. (arguments: target)

container: Run containers on this machine with podman (run an image, run a command inside a running container, stop it, read its logs, list what is running, list local images, pull one) and start/stop nspawn machines with machinectl. A container started with display=x11 draws on this desktop, and the ui_elements tool is what drives it by name with a visible cursor; this tool starts it, and stops it. Needs 'container-control-enabled', off by default. (arguments: action, image, name, command, detach, display, share_bus, publish, all, tail)

login_history: Recent logins to this machine: which user, from which terminal or remote address, when they started and how long they lasted, and recent reboots. Use for 'who logged in', 'has anyone used my computer'. Requires the 'sessions-sense-enabled' consent key, because it reports other people's presence. Read-only. (arguments: limit)

held_out.positives_desc: set_scaling: Report or change the desktop's text scaling factor (1.0 is normal, 1.5 is 150%). Text scaling only - display-resolution and HiDPI scaling are not changed by this, because driving those black-screens sessions. Requires the 'appearance-control-enabled' consent key; reporting needs no such permission. (arguments: action, factor)

negatives.desc: desktop_setting: Read or change one desktop setting from a fixed list: animations (window and menu animations); cursor_size (mouse pointer size in pixels (24 is normal; 32, 48, 64 are larger)); single_click (open files and folders with a single click); clock_24h (show the top-bar clock in 24-hour format); clock_seconds (show seconds in the top-bar clock); battery_percentage (show the battery percentage in the top bar); hot_corner (open the overview when the pointer hits the top-left corner); natural_scroll (touchpad natural (reverse) scrolling); tap_to_click (tap the touchpad to click). Changing requires the 'appearance-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: setting, value)

generate_image: Make a new picture from a text description, or change a photo the way a description says (from_photo, e.g. 'make it snowy', 'as a watercolour'), drawn locally by stable-diffusion.cpp. Describe it in English. Saves a PNG and returns its path. (arguments: prompt, avoid, size, steps, seed, output, from_photo, strength)

undo_last_change: Put a file back the way Chronoa last found it, by restoring the content recorded just before Chronoa's own last edit to it. Undoes Chronoa's recent writes only - NOT git history, NOT changes you made in an editor or a shell, and only while a recorded pre-image is still held. Requires the 'file-edit-enabled' consent key. (arguments: path, list, steps)
encode_text: Encode or decode text: base64, url (percent-encoding), hex, binary, rot13, morse. (arguments: text, scheme, direction)
type_text: Type text at the currently focused window. Requires the 'input-control-enabled' consent key (separate from the vision sense) to be enabled. (arguments: text)
read_text_file: Read a text file and return its contents, optionally a range of lines. Use this to see what a file actually says. (arguments: path, start_line, max_lines)

translate_text: Translate text into another language, using a local translation tool when one is installed and a web service otherwise. The reply says which was used, because one sends your text to a third party. (arguments: text, to_language, from_language)

write_text_file: Write text to a file, creating it or replacing its contents. Refuses to replace a non-empty file unless asked to overwrite, and refuses binary data. (arguments: path, content, overwrite, append)

held_out.say: Ask questions of a spreadsheet or CSV, and chart it.
held_out.positives_desc: analyze_table: Ask questions of a .csv, .tsv, .xlsx or .json (list of records) file with read-only SQLite SQL. describe: the tables, columns, types, row counts and a sample - do this first. query: run one SELECT (the table is `data`, or one table per sheet name for a workbook); save_as='~/x.csv' or .xlsx keeps the full result. chart: bar, line or pie chart saved as .svg from a SELECT returning (label, value) columns. (arguments: action, path, sql, save_as, kind, title, output)

negatives.desc: ask_user: Ask the user a clarifying question and wait for their answer, with 2 to 4 short options they can pick. Use this whenever a request is genuinely ambiguous - especially when several files or devices could match. Do not guess instead, and do not ask when one option is obviously right. In a headless session there is nobody to answer and this will say so. (arguments: question, options)

json_query: Ask questions about the shape of a JSON document: what keys it has, what a field contains, how many entries an array has, or the sum/unique/sorted values of an array. Give either a file path or paste the document itself. (arguments: path, document, field, operation, of)

office_document: Word (.docx), Excel (.xlsx) and PowerPoint (.pptx) files; also reads .odt/.ods/.odp. read: text with headings, tables, one section per sheet or slide (sheet, cell_range like A1:D20, formulas=true to see formulas). create: a new file from content - for .docx Markdown-style text (# headings, - bullets, 1. lists, | tables |, **bold**); for .xlsx rows (list of lists), or sheets {name: rows}, or CSV/Markdown-table text in content, '=...' cells are formulas; for .pptx slides [{title, bullets[], subtitle}]. set_cells: values {'B12': 42, 'C1': 'Total'} in a sheet. replace_text / append: change a .docx. pdf_images: save a PDF's embedded pictures to a folder. Changing an existing file needs 'file-edit-enabled' and can be undone with undo_last_change. (arguments: action, path, content, rows, sheets, slides, values, sheet, cell_range, formulas, find, replace, title, overwrite, output_dir)

fingerprint_status: Whether fingerprint login is set up on this machine, and which fingers are enrolled. Says which of the four real states it is in: no reader attached, reader present but nothing enrolled, fingers enrolled, or the daemon not running and the question unanswerable. Reading only - it never enrolls or deletes a fingerprint, because 'which fingers are enrolled' is a question and the other two are not. Needs no permission: it reports a machine's own login configuration, and the answer is about hardware and a per-user setting rather than anything private. (arguments: user)

list_processes: List the processes running on this machine, with their pid, name, owner, CPU and memory use, sorted by CPU unless sort_by says otherwise. Use this to find what is using the machine - pass sort_by='memory' for the RAM question, which CPU order does not answer - or the pid of something you want to stop. (arguments: name_filter, sort_by, limit)

manage_goals: Save a multi-step goal as a plan of tool steps that can be run later from the Goals panel, list saved goals, answer one that is waiting for you, or remove one. Saving runs nothing. Each step names a tool, its arguments, and a name for its result; a later step can use an earlier result as $name in a string argument, and lists the names it depends_on. A depends_on name that no earlier step produces is a question for the user: the goal waits there until they answer it. Requires the 'goals-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, goal, steps, id, answer)

web_search: Look something up on the web and return what the pages actually say: facts, prices, how-tos, anything no more specific tool covers. Give a search query, a specific URL, or both. For a scholarly question - a paper, a preprint, prior work, 'what does the research say' - set source=arxiv and it searches the arXiv preprint archive instead of the web. For news headlines use news; to click, fill in or book something on a site use browse. Requires the web sense to be enabled and privacy mode to be off. (arguments: query, url, source)

held_out.positives_desc: create_directory: Create a directory, and any missing parent directories. Succeeds without complaint if it already exists. (arguments: path)

negatives.desc: list_directory: List the files and folders in a directory, with each one's type and size. Use this to see what is in a folder before opening, moving or deleting anything in it. (arguments: path, include_hidden)

create_archive: Create a zip or tar.gz archive from files or folders, or list or safely extract an existing one. Refuses archives whose entries would escape the destination. (arguments: action, source, destination, format)

create_video: Create a video: a slideshow from a list of pictures (each shown for a few seconds), or a simple clip of a colour for a duration. Writes a new .mp4 next to the inputs; never overwrites. (arguments: images, seconds, color, duration, width)
create_document: Create a document from a title and body: a markdown file, a plain text file, or an HTML page. Writes a new file; never overwrites. (arguments: title, body, format, path)

lab_network_create: Build an isolated lab network on this machine: a network namespace holding a bridge, with named subnets in namespaces of their own. A public subnet can reach the internet through the uplink; a private one can reach this network and nothing beyond it. Returns the exact plan and changes nothing unless apply=true, which needs your system password. (arguments: name, cidr, subnets, internet, apply)

directory_tree: Show the shape of a directory as a nested tree, with each entry's type. Use this to understand how a project or folder is laid out before opening files in it. Reports what it skipped and when it stopped early. (arguments: path, max_depth, include_hidden)

empty_directories: Find directories under a path that hold nothing at all. Use for 'clean up empty folders', 'what are these leftover directories', 'tidy this up'. Empty means rmdir would succeed - a directory holding only sub-directories is not empty - and one that cannot be read is not empty either. Reports what it found and removes nothing. Read-only. (arguments: path, limit)

held_out.say: Record a short video from the camera.
held_out.positives_desc: capture_video: Record a short video from the camera (webcam), e.g. '/dev/video0', for a few seconds. Requires the vision/camera consent. Writes a new .mp4; no camera means a clear refusal. (arguments: device, seconds, infrared)

negatives.desc: convert_media: Convert an audio, video or image file to another format (mp3, ogg, opus, wav, flac, m4a, mp4, webm, gif, png, jpg, webp), optionally resizing to a width. Writes a new file next to the original; never overwrites. (arguments: path, to, width)

photo_video: Blur or pixelate faces, blur or remove the background, or find people and objects in a photo or video. Works by what is in it, on this computer. identify: find faces and everyday objects (people, cars, dogs, cups...); effect: blur_faces, pixelate_faces, blur_background or remove_background, saved as a new file (videos keep their sound); keyframes: save the moments a video changes; describe: say what happens in a video. For a look like sepia or sketch, or resizing and converting, use edit_image or convert_media. (arguments: action, path, effect, subject, labelled_copy)

media_control: Control music and video players: play, pause, toggle, next track, previous track, stop, restart (current track from the beginning), seek (skip ahead or go back by 'seconds'; negative goes back), or 'status' to say what is playing. (arguments: action, seconds)

read_video: Read a video's basics out loud (for subtitles or what was said use recording): how long it is, its resolution, its video codec, whether it has audio, and its bitrate. Add keyframes=true to also save the moments the image changes. The original is never modified. (arguments: path, keyframes)

recording: Make subtitles or a transcript of a video or audio file, tell speakers apart, or remove background noise. Works on the sound, on this computer. text: what was said; subtitles: save an .srt beside it; speakers: who said what, turn by turn; clean: a copy with background noise removed; sounds: what can be heard in it (music, a dog, traffic...); listen: what can be heard around the computer right now (the microphone, a few seconds); streams: which applications are carrying audio right now, and the name to capture one by (a call in a browser is one); capture: record one of those for 5-600 seconds and transcribe it - which records the room, so it needs the sound consent like the microphone does. (arguments: action, path, language, people, seconds)
convert_color: Convert a colour between hex (#ff8800), rgb(255, 136, 0), hsl and its CSS name. (arguments: color)

convert_currency: Convert an amount of money between currencies (rupees, dollars, euros, pounds, yen, ...) at today's ECB reference rate. Requires the web sense and privacy mode off. (arguments: amount, from_currency, to_currency)

held_out.positives_desc: delete_file: Delete a file or folder by moving it to the desktop trash, where it stays recoverable. This is how you clear something out. The whole folder goes as one item and can be restored from the trash - nothing in this project is deleted permanently, so there is no faster or 'real' delete to reach for instead. Requires the 'file-delete-enabled' consent key. (arguments: path)

negatives.desc: alarm: Alarm clock: set an alarm at a time of day (once, or repeating daily/weekdays/weekends/chosen days), list alarms, say when the next one is, change one's time or label, snooze the one that just rang, or delete one. Examples: 'set an alarm for 7am', 'alarm for 6:30 on weekdays', 'when is my next alarm?', 'change my 7am alarm to 7:30', 'snooze', 'delete the 7am alarm'. Times may be words ('7am', '7:30 pm', 'tomorrow 6:45'). It rings with a notification and the alarm sound even if the assistant is closed; it is held by systemd --user, so a reboot drops it until alarms are next listed, which re-arms it. (arguments: action, time, label, repeat, id, new_time, new_label, minutes)

conversations: The user's saved Chronoa conversations. list: recent ones; search: find what was said in earlier conversations (query); open: continue one (which = title or id); new: start a fresh one; rename (which, title); copy: duplicate one to try another way, optionally keeping only its first keep_turns user messages; export: save one as Markdown (path); delete: remove one permanently (needs 'file-delete-enabled'). (arguments: action, which, query, title, path, keep_turns)

empty_trash: Permanently delete everything in the desktop trash, after listing what is in there first. There is no way to undo this, so it requires the 'trash-empty-enabled' consent key. Use 'list' to see the contents without emptying anything. (arguments: action)

open_files: Find which programs have a file, directory or network socket open. Use for 'what is using this file', 'why can't I delete this', 'what has my disk open', 'which process is holding that socket'. Names the holding program with its full command line, and flags deleted files whose space cannot be reclaimed. Reads only this user's processes unless run as root. Read-only: it lists open handles and never closes one. (arguments: path, pid, limit)

press_key: Press a key or key combination in the focused window, e.g. 'Return', 'Escape', 'Tab' or 'ctrl+shift+t'. This sends a key, not text - use type_text to type a string. Requires the 'input-control-enabled' consent key. X11 only. (arguments: key, repeat)

routines: Save a routine: a short phrase (e.g. 'good morning', 'leaving work') that later runs a whole request, e.g. 'tell me the weather, my calendar today and the top news'. Also list or delete routines. Saving runs nothing; saying the phrase later runs the request. (arguments: action, name, request, phrases)

stale_files: Find files that are both large and untouched for a long time - the deletion candidates a disk-usage answer only gestures at. Use for 'what can I delete', 'what is safe to clean up', 'what in here is old and big'. Reports candidates only: it claims nothing is safe to delete, removes nothing, and says that an untouched timestamp is not proof a file is unused. Read-only. (arguments: path, older_than_days, limit)

held_out.positives_desc: list_apps: List the applications installed on this machine, optionally filtered by a search term, so a request to open something can be answered with what actually exists rather than a guess. (arguments: search)

negatives.desc: open_application: Open or launch an installed application by name or by kind, e.g. 'firefox', 'files', 'settings', 'music player', 'text editor'. Not for websites: use browse to open a site and work on it. (arguments: name)

install_app: Search Flathub for an app, or install / remove one for this user by its app ID (e.g. org.videolan.VLC, from a search). Installing and removing need the 'app-install-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, query, app_id)

install_model: Download a named model into the local Ollama. Takes an explicit model name and never picks one by itself - call recommend_model first and install only what the user agreed to. Warns rather than refuses when the model looks larger than available memory. This downloads gigabytes and needs the network. (arguments: name)

list_windows: List the windows currently open, with their title, class and geometry. Pass title_contains to narrow the list to windows matching some text in their title or application - a desktop usually has more windows open than are worth reading. Where xdotool cannot see the session it falls back to the accessibility bus and says so, because that list is not complete. (arguments: title_contains)

list_capabilities: Report what this assistant can do right now, and which of those need a setting switched on first. Reads the live skill registry and the live consent values rather than a fixed list, so a skill that is not installed, or a permission that is off, is shown as such. Changes nothing.

list_fonts: List the font families installed on this machine (optionally only those whose name contains some text), and which real font the generic names - sans-serif, serif, monospace, emoji - or a font you name actually resolve to. Use for 'what fonts do I have', 'is Fira Code installed', 'which font is used for monospace'. Read-only. (arguments: query)

close_window: Ask a window to close, the way its close button would - the application still gets the chance to ask about unsaved work. Requires the 'window-close-enabled' consent key. Works on X11, Plasma and GNOME (GTK4 apps, or any app with Chronoa's window control extension). (arguments: window_id, title_contains)

held_out.positives_desc: print_file: Print a document file on the default printer, or on a named one. Refuses directories and non-document files. Reports the job as queued, since whether it actually printed is not observable from here. (arguments: path, printer)

negatives.desc: print_queue: Show the printers, which one is the default, the print jobs still waiting, and what this machine can print to even when nothing is configured; or cancel a waiting job by its id. Use for 'what's printing', 'why isn't my printer there', 'what can I print to', 'cancel that print'. Cancelling requires the 'print-control-enabled' consent key; listing does not. (arguments: action, job, printer, option)

delete_file: Delete a file or folder by moving it to the desktop trash, where it stays recoverable. This is how you clear something out. The whole folder goes as one item and can be restored from the trash - nothing in this project is deleted permanently, so there is no faster or 'real' delete to reach for instead. Requires the 'file-delete-enabled' consent key. (arguments: path)

download_file: Download a file from a web address and save it to disk, reporting the size and how long it took. Use for 'download that file', 'get this installer', 'save that page'. Only http and https; a site that answers with an error page reports that rather than saving the error as if it were the file. (arguments: url, destination)

edit_file: Replace one exact piece of text in one named file. The text to replace must appear exactly once, or nothing is written - the count and line numbers are reported instead of a guess being made. Use this to change a specific line; use find_and_replace to change a string across many files. Requires the 'file-edit-enabled' consent key. (arguments: path, old_string, new_string, preview, replace_all)

file_locks: Show who holds a file lock, and on what - the answer to "why won't this file save" and "why did my write fail with EAGAIN". A WRITE lock blocks another writer; a READ lock is shared and usually harmless. Use for 'who has this file locked', 'what is holding a lock', 'why can't I write this file', 'is this file locked'. Give a path to check one file; omit it for every lock on the machine. Reads the kernel's own lock table (/proc/locks), so it needs no binary and no privilege. Read-only; nothing is polled, changed or broken. (arguments: path)

get_file_info: Report one file's type, size, when it was last modified, and who can read it. Use this to answer 'when did I last edit this' or 'who else can read this file' - no other skill reports timestamps or permissions. (arguments: path)

identify_file: Identify a file by reading its first bytes rather than trusting its name. Use for 'why won't this open', 'what is this file', 'is this really a PNG', 'this file has no extension'. Reports the detected format and whether the filename agrees with it, which is the usual cause of a file refusing to open in the program its name implies. Says plainly when a signature is unrecognised. Read-only. (arguments: path)

held_out.positives_desc: convert_color: Convert a colour between hex (#ff8800), rgb(255, 136, 0), hsl and its CSS name. (arguments: color)

negatives.desc: ir_remote: Send and receive infrared remote-control codes, and build or read the pulse-space timings themselves. 'devices': is there IR hardware here (most machines have none, and that is a true answer). 'encode': turn an address and command into the NEC or RC-6 timings that would carry them. 'decode': turn timings into a code. 'send': transmit a code through an IR device. 'receive': capture a button press and decode it. Needs the 'ir-remote-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, protocol, address, command, timings, seconds)

create_video: Create a video: a slideshow from a list of pictures (each shown for a few seconds), or a simple clip of a colour for a duration. Writes a new .mp4 next to the inputs; never overwrites. (arguments: images, seconds, color, duration, width)

read_image: Read a picture's basics out loud: width by height, format, and colour type, plus file size. For what the picture says, use read_document on it. The original is never modified. (arguments: path)

held_out.say: Is fingerprint login set up on this machine?
held_out.positives_desc: fingerprint_status: Whether fingerprint login is set up on this machine, and which fingers are enrolled. Says which of the four real states it is in: no reader attached, reader present but nothing enrolled, fingers enrolled, or the daemon not running and the question unanswerable. Reading only - it never enrolls or deletes a fingerprint, because 'which fingers are enrolled' is a question and the other two are not. Needs no permission: it reports a machine's own login configuration, and the answer is about hardware and a per-user setting rather than anything private. (arguments: user)

negatives.desc: login_history: Recent logins to this machine: which user, from which terminal or remote address, when they started and how long they lasted, and recent reboots. Use for 'who logged in', 'has anyone used my computer'. Requires the 'sessions-sense-enabled' consent key, because it reports other people's presence. Read-only. (arguments: limit)

set_locale: Report the system language and regional formats, list the locales available on this machine, or change one: the system language, or the date format (British day/month or American month/day order), number format (decimal comma or point), money, measurement or paper size (e.g. what='dates', locale='en_GB.UTF-8'). Takes effect at the next login. Changing requires the 'locale-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, locale, what)

set_power_profile: Switch the machine between its power profiles - typically power-saver, balanced and performance - and report which one is active now. The profile list is read from the machine rather than assumed, because which profiles exist depends on the CPU driver: switching to one the machine does not have is refused with the valid names listed. Changes the CPU and platform power behaviour, not a per-application setting. (arguments: profile)

set_privacy: Control the machine's privacy: mute or unmute the microphone, enable or disable a camera, or blank the screen. Muting the microphone is a user-level stream mute that any new application can override, and the reply says so rather than implying the hardware is off. Disabling a camera needs root and is only possible on drivers that expose a disable control, so a device with no such control is reported as unsupported rather than disabled. Blanking works on X11; under Wayland it would need a permission prompt, so the idle timeout is offered instead. Every action says how to undo it. (arguments: action, device)

set_screensaver: Report or change how long the machine waits before the screen blanks, and whether it then demands a password. The two are reported separately, because blanking without locking leaves anyone who walks up to the machine able to use it. Requires the 'idle-timeout-enabled' consent key; reporting needs no such permission. (arguments: action, blank_after_minutes, lock)

set_sleep_inhibit: Report what is currently holding the machine awake, or take a bounded hold so it does not sleep for a while, or release ours. Use for 'keep it awake while I...' - a long install, a backup, a test run. Scoped and self-lapsing; to change the machine's idle timeout permanently use set_screensaver instead. Gated by 'sleep-inhibit-enabled' consent key; reporting needs no such permission. (arguments: action, reason, seconds)

autostart_entries: Report everything on this machine that starts automatically: the autostart .desktop files in this user's home and /etc/xdg, the enabled systemd user units and timers, and the crontab. Use for 'what starts automatically', 'what runs at login', 'what is scheduled', 'why does this thing keep running', 'what did I set to start on its own'. Honours Hidden, OnlyShowIn and NotShowIn, and says 'cannot tell' rather than guessing when the desktop is unknown - which is the normal state outside a login session. Read-only; nothing is enabled, disabled or changed.

held_out.positives_desc: crash_report: Programs that crashed recently on this machine (core dumps recorded by systemd-coredump): which program, when, and the signal that killed it. Use for 'what crashed', 'why did that app close'. Uses the 'coredumps-sense-enabled' switch. Read-only.

negatives.desc: find_recently_modified: List files under a directory whose recorded modification time is within the last N days, newest first. Use this to answer 'what did I change today'. This is a timestamp, so a tool that preserves or sets times (tar, rsync, cp -p) can move an entry without the content changing. (arguments: path, within_days, pattern, limit)

boot_report: How the last boot went: total boot time split into firmware, loader, kernel and userspace, the services that took longest to start, when the machine booted and whether it shut down cleanly before, and which EFI entry the firmware will boot by default. Use for 'why does it boot slowly', 'did it crash last time'. Boot history uses the 'boots-sense-enabled' switch. Read-only. (arguments: top)

graphics_stack: Report whether OpenGL is hardware accelerated or falling back to software (llvmpipe). Answers from sysfs for the kernel driver - always, with no display needed - and from glxinfo -B for the renderer string, which is the only thing that actually says hardware or software. Use for 'is my graphics accelerated', 'why is this game slow', 'is my GPU being used', 'what graphics card renderer am I on'. Says which of the two it could not read and why, and never reports a crashed tool as a fact about the GPU. Read-only; nothing is changed.

held_out.positives_desc: scan_document: Scan a page and return its text (OCR), keeping the image in ~/Documents/Scans. source: 'scanner' (default; list_only lists them), 'camera' (hold the page up to the webcam; it is found and straightened), or 'photo' (straighten and read a picture of a page at path). 'Scan this letter and read it to me.' (arguments: source, path, list_only, device)

negatives.desc: nfc: Read and write NFC tags. 'scan': is there a reader here (most laptops have none, and that is a true answer). 'read': tap a tag and be told what is written on it. 'write': put a link on an Ultralight/NTAG sticker - a bank card, transit pass or hotel key is refused, not rewritten. 'emulate': present a tag to a phone. Needs the 'nfc-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, url, text, seconds, target)

scan_network: Find which devices are on the local network, with their names, addresses and hardware vendors. Local addresses only. Requires the network sense to be enabled. (arguments: range, resolve_names)

fm_radio: FM and AM broadcast radio. Five actions: 'hardware' for whether this computer can receive anything at all (a laptop usually cannot, and that is a true answer rather than a failure - it needs an RTL2832U USB dongle), 'bands' for the coverage, 'tune' to a frequency, 'decode' to demodulate a recorded IQ capture, and 'scan' to look for carriers in one. A frequency is given in MHz, e.g. 98.6. rtl_fm is narrowband and retunes per channel, so it cannot scan - scanning needs a wideband recording. No station names are guessed: a carrier gives a frequency, and naming it would need a table for your region. Requires the 'fm-radio-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, frequency, seconds, file, centre_mhz, out, deemphasis_us)

read_document: Read the text of a PDF (optionally a page range) or of an image (OCR), e.g. to summarise it or read it out. For a PDF it also reports whether the document embeds its fonts, since one that does not prints wrong elsewhere. (arguments: path, first_page, last_page)

browse: Open a website and do things on it for the person: find information, fill in forms, click through. Drive a web browser: navigate, read the page's text (get_text), click, type, select options, scroll, move through history, take screenshots and wait for conditions. While Chronoa's window is open this is the in-app browser the user can watch: there it opens only http(s) pages the egress policy allows, and key, hover, drag, upload_file, tabs and evaluate are not available. Otherwise it is a headless Chromium with all actions. Requires the web sense to be enabled and privacy mode to be off. (arguments: action, url, selector, text, key, value, label, files, x, y, to_x, to_y, to_selector, delta_x, delta_y, steps, repeat, tab_id, path, wait_for, timeout, settle)

process_cost: What each running program is COSTING this machine right now, measured over the last second rather than as a snapshot: percent CPU split into user and system time, how much memory it holds, page faults (including the major ones that mean it is thrashing), and how many kB a second it is reading and writing. Answers 'what is using my CPU', 'what is making my computer slow', 'what is writing to my disk all the time', 'which program is swapping', 'why did everything freeze'. Use this when the machine feels slow; use list_processes to see what is running and disk_activity to see whether the disk itself is busy. Read-only; nothing is started, stopped or changed.

web_search: Look something up on the web and return what the pages actually say: facts, prices, how-tos, anything no more specific tool covers. Give a search query, a specific URL, or both. For a scholarly question - a paper, a preprint, prior work, 'what does the research say' - set source=arxiv and it searches the arXiv preprint archive instead of the web. For news headlines use news; to click, fill in or book something on a site use browse. Requires the web sense to be enabled and privacy mode to be off. (arguments: query, url, source)

held_out.positives_desc: manage_mount: Mount an unmounted filesystem or drive, or unmount one, through the desktop's own disk service so its authorisation rules apply. Verifies the result against the mount table. Requires the 'mount-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, device)

negatives.desc: check_units: Check whether systemd unit files are valid and say what is wrong with them - a missing ExecStart binary, an unknown key, a dependency that does not exist - by running systemd-analyze verify on just the units you name. With no unit named, lists the services this machine has. This is a static check of the file: it does not know whether a dependency is down or a path is mounted, so a clean report does not promise the service will start. Reading only; nothing is started, stopped or changed. (arguments: unit)

disk_health: Health of this machine's drives (SMART/NVMe status and wear where it can be read) and whether each mounted filesystem - /, /home and the rest - sits on an encrypted (LUKS) volume. Use for 'is my SSD healthy', 'is my disk encrypted', 'how worn is my drive'. Drive health uses the 'storage-sense-enabled' switch. Read-only.

disk_layout: Show how this machine's disks are partitioned: every physical disk, each partition with its size, filesystem and purpose (EFI, Linux root, /home, LUKS, LVM, swap), and where each one is mounted. Use for 'how is my disk partitioned', 'what partitions are on this machine', 'which partition is my home directory on', 'is my disk GPT or plain', 'what is this LUKS partition for'. Follows the storage sense's consent switch, because it reports the same machine. Read-only; nothing is changed. Loop devices (the immutable snap images) are hidden unless show_hidden is set, and their count is always stated. (arguments: show_hidden)

device_probe: What user-space driver routes this machine has: I2C buses, video devices, and FUSE mounts. Read-only, and reports unknown-with-a-reason where a list could not be read rather than claiming there is nothing.

held_out.positives_desc: media_control: Control music and video players: play, pause, toggle, next track, previous track, stop, restart (current track from the beginning), seek (skip ahead or go back by 'seconds'; negative goes back), or 'status' to say what is playing. (arguments: action, seconds)

negatives.desc: convert_media: Convert an audio, video or image file to another format (mp3, ogg, opus, wav, flac, m4a, mp4, webm, gif, png, jpg, webp), optionally resizing to a width. Writes a new file next to the original; never overwrites. (arguments: path, to, width)

open_application: Open or launch an installed application by name or by kind, e.g. 'firefox', 'files', 'settings', 'music player', 'text editor'. Not for websites: use browse to open a site and work on it. (arguments: name)

phone_remote: Press keys on the paired phone as a Bluetooth keyboard: 'press' the camera 'shutter' (takes a photo in the camera app), play_pause, next, previous, volume_up/down, mute; or 'type' text into whatever field is focused on the phone. The phone must have paired 'Chronoa Remote'. Requires the 'phone-remote-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, key, text)

set_timer: Set a countdown timer that sends a desktop notification when it finishes; list pending timers, say how much time is left, add or take off time, pause, resume, reset to the original length, and cancel. With one timer pending, 'my timer' needs no id. The countdown is owned by systemd, so it fires even if the assistant is closed. It is refused rather than silently accepted when systemd is unavailable, because a timer recorded as pending that will never fire is the same lie as a camera reported as disabled when it is not. (arguments: action, seconds, label, id)

recording: Make subtitles or a transcript of a video or audio file, tell speakers apart, or remove background noise. Works on the sound, on this computer. text: what was said; subtitles: save an .srt beside it; speakers: who said what, turn by turn; clean: a copy with background noise removed; sounds: what can be heard in it (music, a dog, traffic...); listen: what can be heard around the computer right now (the microphone, a few seconds); streams: which applications are carrying audio right now, and the name to capture one by (a call in a browser is one); capture: record one of those for 5-600 seconds and transcribe it - which records the room, so it needs the sound consent like the microphone does. (arguments: action, path, language, people, seconds)

list_shortcuts: List this machine's keyboard shortcuts, or find what one key does. Reads GNOME's two keybinding schemas, so it covers both window management and the hardware media keys, and reports that the scheme does not apply on a desktop that does not use it rather than listing defaults for a desktop that is not running. Reading a shortcut is not a change and needs no permission. (arguments: action, keys)

photo_video: Blur or pixelate faces, blur or remove the background, or find people and objects in a photo or video. Works by what is in it, on this computer. identify: find faces and everyday objects (people, cars, dogs, cups...); effect: blur_faces, pixelate_faces, blur_background or remove_background, saved as a new file (videos keep their sound); keyframes: save the moments a video changes; describe: say what happens in a video. For a look like sepia or sketch, or resizing and converting, use edit_image or convert_media. (arguments: action, path, effect, subject, labelled_copy)

held_out.say: Run a quick alpine container that prints hello.
held_out.positives_desc: container: Run containers on this machine with podman (run an image, run a command inside a running container, stop it, read its logs, list what is running, list local images, pull one) and start/stop nspawn machines with machinectl. A container started with display=x11 draws on this desktop, and the ui_elements tool is what drives it by name with a visible cursor; this tool starts it, and stops it. Needs 'container-control-enabled', off by default. (arguments: action, image, name, command, detach, display, share_bus, publish, all, tail)

negatives.desc: list_containers: List this machine's containers: distroboxes (by name, with their image and whether they are running) and podman/docker containers, including any that exited because they ran out of memory, plus how much disk the images use. Use for 'what distroboxes do I have', 'is my container running', 'why did my container die'. The podman details use the 'containers-sense-enabled' switch. Read-only.

print_file: Print a document file on the default printer, or on a named one. Refuses directories and non-document files. Reports the job as queued, since whether it actually printed is not observable from here. (arguments: path, printer)

print_queue: Show the printers, which one is the default, the print jobs still waiting, and what this machine can print to even when nothing is configured; or cancel a waiting job by its id. Use for 'what's printing', 'why isn't my printer there', 'what can I print to', 'cancel that print'. Cancelling requires the 'print-control-enabled' consent key; listing does not. (arguments: action, job, printer, option)

explain_command: Explain a Linux shell command (not a general topic) from the local manuals (tldr, man), e.g. 'what does tar do', 'how do I use rsync'; or find which command does something, e.g. 'which command shows disk usage'. (arguments: command, task)

manage_triggers: Arm, list, or remove automatic rules that run a Chronoa action when a perception matches - for example, notify when the battery sense reports low. A rule names one already-whitelisted skill; it cannot run an arbitrary command or an LLM-authored prompt. Listing needs no permission; arming or disarming requires the 'trigger-control-enabled' consent key. (arguments: action, name, sense, match_mode, substring, keywords, actuator, arguments, cooldown_seconds, event_type, source, params, ask_first, retry_policy, debounce_seconds)

ui_elements: Use another app's controls by what they are, through the accessibility tree. apps: which apps are reachable. inspect: list a window's buttons, fields, menus and labels with ids (app = its name; query narrows by text). press: activate an element by id (a button, checkbox, link, menu item). set_text: put text in a field by id. read: an element's text or value. menu: open a menu path like 'File > Export'. drive: one turn of driving - give an action and a control number and the reply is the app's new state in the same short numbered form, which is what a small model can act on. act: click, type or key an app by name or position, with a visible cursor. state: the numbered controls an app is showing. Works on a container's app and on this desktop's own apps alike. Requires 'input-control-enabled'; drive start also runs a container, so it needs 'container-control-enabled' as well. (arguments: action, app, id, text, query, path, do, how, number, image, keys, x, y)
